chunk_findings.detail: The new malformed-call test uses `isinstance(exc, TypeError)` while it uses exact-type tests (`type(exc) in (KeyError, ValueError)`) for the other two, even though the new docstring in `core/outcome.py` states only "a **bare** Key/Type/ValueError" is a malformed call and "a subclass keeps its own exit". `isinstance` matches every `TypeError` subclass, so a class such as `class ArgTypeError(TypeError): exit_code = FAIL` is now collapsed to `bad arguments: ...` with no `meta.exit`, even though `outcome.exit_for` returned its declared `FAIL` and the outcome layer's own contract is "a class declares its own exit with `exit_code`". This is also a regression against the pre-change code, which checked `getattr(type(exc), "exit_code", None) is not None` *before* the `isinstance(exc, TypeError)` fallback; before this diff such a class returned `str(exc)` with `error=True, meta={"exit": code}`. To honor the stated "bare ... a subclass keeps its own exit" rule and the declared-`exit_code` precedence, the predicate should test `type(exc) is TypeError` (i.e. `type(exc) in (TypeError, KeyError, ValueError)`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:728

chunk_findings.detail: The guard can only change the outcome for `TypeError` (or a subclass) or an exact-type `KeyError`/`ValueError` that declares `exit_code`. But the two non-`bad arguments` symptoms named in the task — `GitError` "reach[ing] mcp.py:1598 as an internal error" and the "uncaught LeaseError" — are by the task's own description *not* labeled `bad arguments`, i.e. they are exceptions that fall outside this branch (a `GitError` mapped to an internal error means `exit_for(exc)` returned `None`, since if it returned any code the pre-existing fall-through would have returned, not raised). For such an exception the new code is a no-op: `code = exit_for(exc)` is still `None`, the `undeclared and (...)` condition is not even evaluated for it, and `if code is None: raise` still fires, so a tool raising `GitError`/`LeaseError` still surfaces as an internal error. This diff touches only `mcp.py` and the test file — no production exception class is given an `exit_code` and `exit_for` is not extended — so the only new behavior is for the test-local `ArgTypeError(TypeError)` class, and the `GitError`/`LeaseError` half of the reported bug is left unfixed. A regression test for the actual reported symptom (call a tool that raises `GitError` and assert it is not an internal error) would still fail after this change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:728 (the new `undeclared` guard)

chunk_findings.detail:
The regression test does not actually exercise the changed branch, so it does not demonstrate the bug it claims to fix. Before this change `exit_for` already walked `_EXIT_BY_NAME` over the MRO (the removed loop), so for the test's `Named(ValueError)` with `_EXIT_BY_NAME[...] = REFUSED`, the unfixed `exit_for` already returns `REFUSED`. In mcp.py the very next line is `if code == REFUSED: return _ok(...)`, which returns before the modified "bad arguments" condition is reached. So on the unfixed code `_call_raising(repo, monkeypatch, Named("named refusal"))` already yields `reply["result"]["_meta"]["exit"] == O.REFUSED` with no "bad arguments"; the test only fails because `O.declared_exit` does not yet exist (AttributeError). Concretely: add `declared_exit` but revert the mcp.py hunk and the MCP assertions of this test still pass — it guards nothing about the mcp change.

Worse, the mcp hunk cannot fix the stated bug either. The guard is `isinstance(exc, TypeError) or type(exc) in (KeyError, ValueError)`. For `ReviewerRefused`, "a ValueError" per the intent, `isinstance(exc, TypeError)` is False and `type(exc) in (KeyError, ValueError)` is an exact-type test that is False for any subclass, so the "bad arguments" label was already unreachable for it in the old code. The new `declared_exit(exc) is None` condition can only change behavior for a `TypeError` subclass whose class is registered in `_EXIT_BY_NAME` (the table as shown contains only `GitError`), so the reported mislabeling of `ReviewerRefused` remains unaddressed.

chunk_findings.detail:
The modified branch cannot change `ReviewerRefused`'s exit, so it cannot fix B5f3a650c40. It is reached only *after* `code = exit_for(exc)` and the early `if code == REFUSED: return _ok(mid, _text(str(exc), meta={"exit": REFUSED}))`, and only when `declared_exit(exc) is None`. A refusal declares `REFUSED` (the outcome docstring: "every refusal: `REFUSED`"), so `exit_for` already returned `REFUSED` and the pre-existing REFUSED branch returned the refusal before this line — the edit is dead code for the reported case. Conversely, if `ReviewerRefused` is an *undeclared* `ValueError` subclass, `isinstance(exc, ValueError)` is now True, so it is routed to `bad arguments` — precisely the mislabelling the bug reports, now made unconditional. Either way the symptom is unchanged, and the correct fix (giving `ReviewerRefused` a `REFUSED` declaration, or mapping it via `_EXIT_BY_NAME`) is absent from the diff.

The widening is also a standalone regression: before this change `type(exc) in (KeyError, ValueError)` deliberately excluded subclasses so a subclass "keeps its own exit"/is surfaced as a bug. Now any undeclared `ValueError`/`KeyError` subclass escaping a tool is reported to the caller as `bad arguments: ...`, i.e. blamed on the client. Given input where a tool fails on the *server's* own data — e.g. `json.loads(server_config)` raising `json.JSONDecodeError`, `bytes.decode()` raising `UnicodeDecodeError`, or `pydantic.ValidationError` from internal model construction — the client now receives "bad arguments" and the server-side defect is masked, which is the same class of error-misattribution the bug is about, only broader.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:728 (`isinstance(exc, (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError))`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts behaviour that is new, not "As before the fix" as its docstring claims, and it does not pin the bug being fixed. On the unfixed code the condition is `isinstance(exc, TypeError) or type(exc) in (KeyError, ValueError)`; for `exc = json.JSONDecodeError("{")` the first disjunct is False and the second is False because `type(exc)` is a `ValueError` *subclass*, so the reply is not `"bad arguments: ..."` and the assertion fails — that is the only reason this counts as a "regression test". It therefore certifies the widening described above rather than `ReviewerRefused → REFUSED`; no test in the diff invokes a `ReviewerRefused` at all, so the reported bug would still manifest (or be newly masked as "bad arguments") with this suite green. Note also that the companion test was switched from a `ValueError` subclass to a `TypeError` subclass even though the `declared_exit(exc) is None` guard already preserves a declared `ValueError` subclass, dropping coverage of the exact refusal-type case the fix claims to address.

chunk_findings.detail: Pre-change, `legacy.scan` labelled an in-repo file with `str(path.relative_to(repo))`, while `export/templates.rel` labelled it with `.as_posix()`; the change routes both through one `repo_rel` implementation, so the two cannot both remain byte-identical on Windows. The added test file makes the contradiction explicit: `tests/test_relpath_labels.py:41` asserts the legacy label equals `_old_label(...)` verbatim (native separators), while `tests/test_relpath_labels.py:60` asserts the template value equals `_old_label(...).replace(os.sep, "/")` (POSIX separators); on Windows those two assertions cannot both hold for the same helper's output, so one of the pinned labels is no longer byte-identical (and that test fails).

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own documentation contradicts the stated requirement that behaviour stay byte-identical. The original docstring stated the labels "print exactly what the old lexical derivation printed, also when the repository is reached through a symlink"; the new one carves out an exception: "except that labels are POSIX text everywhere: on Windows the old legacy.scan label (str(path)) used native separators, now '/' like every repo_rel report." On Windows, `str(path)` for a `WindowsPath` yields backslashes (e.g. `svc\legacy.py`), whereas routing through `repo_relative(..., as_given=True)`/`repo_rel` emits `svc/legacy.py`. So for the concrete input of a Windows host with a repo-relative legacy.py path, `legacy.scan` no longer prints the same bytes it printed before, directly violating "Behaviour must stay byte-identical" in the intent. Any consumer, golden file, or test that compares the legacy label against the previous native-separator output on Windows will observe a different string after this change. Either the production change must preserve the prior separator behaviour on Windows, or the intent's byte-identical claim (and the test's "pins the ... labels" contract) is false and should not be relied on.

chunk_findings.detail:
The change wraps `repo_rel(...)`'s result in `Path(...)` and then calls `str(rel)` at append time. Per the previous revision of this test's own docstring, `repo_rel(as_given=True)` emits POSIX separators on every platform ("now '/' like every repo_rel report"), so on Windows `Path("docs/HANDOFF.md")` is a `WindowsPath` whose `str()` is `docs\HANDOFF.md`. The production label therefore becomes native-separator text on Windows, contradicting the intent's "Behaviour must stay byte-identical". More concretely, the test that pins the labels still asserts the POSIX spelling:

```python
labels = sorted({p.path for p in proposals})
assert labels == [".claude/commands/done.md", "CLAUDE.md", "docs/HANDOFF.md"]
```

On Windows the set now contains `["\.claude\\commands\\done.md", "CLAUDE.md", "docs\\HANDOFF.md"]`, so the `==` at that line fails (the per-label loop below it passes, because `_old_legacy_label` is also native). The environment that demonstrates it is simply running the suite on Windows (the platform the module docstring explicitly discusses); the change makes legacy.scan native but leaves the pinned expectation POSIX, so the test is self-inconsistent there.

chunk_findings.detail: The change routes the label through `repo_relative(repo, path, as_given=True)`, which normalizes `..` segments, whereas the replaced line `path.relative_to(repo) if path.is_relative_to(repo) else path` deliberately trusted the path lexically and never collapsed `..`. The two disagree for any operator-supplied `extra=` entry that names a path under `repo` but contains a `..` component. Concretely, with `extra=["docs/../CLAUDE.md"]` (or the absolute form `str(repo / "docs/../CLAUDE.md")`): `Path(repo / "docs/../CLAUDE.md").is_relative_to(repo)` is True, so the old code produced the label `"docs/../CLAUDE.md"`, while the new helper resolves it to `"CLAUDE.md"`. Likewise two extras `"docs/../CLAUDE.md"` and `"CLAUDE.md"` collapse to the same label now but were distinct strings before, so any downstream label-based dedup/matching sees different bytes. This contradicts the stated invariant “Behaviour must stay byte-identical”, and the change itself concedes the divergence in the new docstring at tests/test_relpath_labels.py:3-5; the test inputs actually used (`"docs/HANDOFF.md"`, `str(repo / "CLAUDE.md")`) contain no `..`, so no assertion exercises the case and the drift ships untested.

data.title: Writers in companions, adopt, enforce, api/rules, services/rules, operations and flowstate go through fsio.atomic_write (follow_symlinks=True where write_text wrote through a link); write_text/tempfile/os_replace ratchets lowered
fsio.read_json(path) -> dict | Unreadable replacing the four JSON-config parsers (claudehooks._read, adopt, launchers x2, harness) that decide differently on invalid JSON

data.body:
Survey 2026-10-06: Also the reading side: fsio.read_json(path) -> dict | Unreadable, replacing four parsers that decide differently on invalid JSON (claudehooks._read, adopt.py:1205, launchers.py:118/148, harness.py:53).

Split into: B-uni-fsio-writers.1-write, B-uni-fsio-writers.2-read-json.

data.claim: Not as atomic_write stands: it differs from Path.write_text in three observable ways - it replaces a symlink with a regular file instead of writing through it (CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md is a common layout adopt writes), it creates missing parent directories where write_text raises FileNotFoundError, and it writes '\n' untranslated where text mode writes os.linesep (Windows CRLF). A write-through, no-mkdir, newline-translating wrapper (fsio.replace_text) keeps every site identical. Separately, api/rules DDFLOW.md and services/rules rule files are written (and rules read) in the LOCALE encoding: a non-ASCII rule fails under an ASCII locale - a bug, fixed by utf-8 both ways.
data.falsifier: atomic_write on a symlink leaves the link in place, or write_text under LC_ALL=C PYTHONUTF8=0 writes a non-ASCII string.
data.mechanism: os.replace(tmp, link) renames over the link itself; Path.write_text opens the link (follows it); open() text mode newline=None translates; write_text() without encoding uses locale.getencoding().
data.probe: scratchpad U2_probe2.py (symlink, missing dir) and U2_enc.py under LC_ALL=C PYTHONUTF8=0 PYTHONCOERCECLOCALE=0
data.probe_output: write_text: link kept: True target: via write_text / atomic_write: link kept: False (link replaced by a regular file) / write_text into missing dir: FileNotFoundError / Path.write_text('café') under C locale: UnicodeEncodeError: 'ascii' codec can't encode character
data.question: Can the write_text/mkstemp writers in companions, adopt, enforce, api/rules, services/rules, operations and flowstate move to fsio.atomic_write with no user-visible change?

data.summary: services/rules.py writes rule TOML with rule_path.write_text(rule.to_toml()) and reads it with read_text() (no encoding), api/rules.py writes DDFLOW.md with write_text(manifest_content): both use the locale encoding. Under an ASCII locale (LC_ALL=C, PYTHONUTF8=0) a rule with a non-ASCII character fails with UnicodeEncodeError, and on Windows (cp1252) the committed rule file is not UTF-8, so a clone on another machine reads it garbled. Fix: utf-8 both ways (found while moving these writers to fsio, B-uni-fsio-writers.1-write).
data.title: Rule files and DDFLOW.md are written and read in the locale encoding

evidence.note: R37ec43d2a4 CONFIRMED: atomic_write replaces a symlink with a regular file and creates missing parents, unlike write_text (probe: link kept False; write_text into missing dir FileNotFoundError); rules written/read in locale encoding fail under LC_ALL=C (UnicodeEncodeError) -> bug Bd5adf89e33. Hence fsio.replace_text (write-through, no mkdir) for the write_text sites.

chunk_findings.detail: The pre-check conflates "parent does not exist" with "parent is not a directory", so it raises the wrong exception type. Given `replace_text("regular_file/child.txt", "x")` where `regular_file` is an existing regular file (not a directory): `named.is_symlink()` swallows the `ENOTDIR` from `lstat` and returns `False`, so `target = named`; `target.parent.is_dir()` is `False` (pathlib's `is_dir` ignores `ENOTDIR`), so the function raises `FileNotFoundError` (ENOENT). `Path("regular_file/child.txt").write_text("x")` instead raises `NotADirectoryError` (ENOTDIR). This directly contradicts the "drop-in for a writer moving off `write_text`" contract in the docstring and changes which `OSError` subclass callers must catch; the check needs to distinguish ENOENT from ENOTDIR (or let `atomic_write` surface it once a genuine only-missing-parent guard is used).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/fsio.py:130 (`if not target.parent.is_dir()`)

chunk_findings.detail: The link-loop detection only fires when `named` itself is a symlink, because `Path.is_symlink()`/`is_dir()` swallow `ELOOP`. Given `/tmp/loop/x` where `/tmp/loop` is a self-referential symlink (`loop -> loop`): `named.is_symlink()` hits `ELOOP` on `lstat` and returns `False`, so `target = named` and `realpath` is never consulted; `target.is_symlink()` likewise returns `False`; `target.parent.is_dir()` (`/tmp/loop`) swallows `ELOOP` and returns `False`; the function raises `FileNotFoundError`. `Path("/tmp/loop/x").write_text("y")` raises `OSError` with `ELOOP`. The docstring's claim that "a link loop raises as `write_text` does" holds only for a loop whose *final* component is the symlink, not for a loop reached through an intermediate path component.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/fsio.py:128 (`if target.is_symlink():`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change promises `Path.write_text(text, "utf-8")` semantics made atomic, and it explicitly handles the symlink case ("writes THROUGH a symlink, link kept"). But an atomic write implemented as `mkstemp` + `os.replace` replaces the *directory entry*, not the inode, so unlike `write_text` it does not write through hard links. Concretely: `ln .ddflow/DDFLOW.md /elsewhere/DDFLOW.md` then run any of the rewritten sites (e.g. adopt's managed-block writer at adopt.py:1020, or `rule_path` writer at adopt.py:905). `Path.write_text` used to truncate the shared inode in place, so both names saw the new content; `replace_text` now creates a fresh inode and `os.replace`s the name, so `/elsewhere/DDFLOW.md` silently keeps the stale content and the two names are no longer linked (nlink drops to 1). The same inode-replacement also drops the file's existing owner, extended ACLs and xattrs (only the mode is re-applied), and requires write permission on the parent directory rather than on the file itself — e.g. a writable rule file sitting in a read-only mounted directory used to be updatable with `write_text` but now raises `PermissionError` from `mkstemp`. `tests/test_fsio.py` compares symlinks/loops/missing parents/modes, so this divergence is untested.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/fsio.py:replace_text (used at ddflow/services/adopt.py:606, 635, 641, 886, 905, 965, 986, 1020, 1023, 1202, 1215)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite calls `atomic_write(path, body, mode=_mode(path), fsync=False)`, and in doing so it evaluates `_mode(path)` *eagerly as a call argument*. In the old body the same call sat inside `with contextlib.suppress(OSError): os.chmod(name, _mode(path))`, i.e. an `OSError` raised while reading the ring's mode was deliberately swallowed, which is what made the "mkstemp makes 0600: keep the ring's mode" comment true for a *not-yet-existing* ring: the chmod (and the `_mode` stat) fails, is suppressed, and the freshly created file stays at mkstemp's 0600. With the new code there is no suppression anywhere: on the very first `_replace` for a repo (fresh checkout, or after `.ddflow/local` is deleted so the ring file does not exist), `_mode(path)` raises `FileNotFoundError`/`OSError` before `atomic_write` is ever entered, so `_replace` aborts and the ring is never created. Even if `_mode` were written defensively, the old file's guarantee that a brand-new ring is created 0600 (private) has been replaced by whatever `atomic_write`'s default/`~umask` policy yields, so the observable permission of a new ring changes. The fix is to compute the mode defensively (e.g. `mode=None if not path.exists() else _mode(path)`, or wrap `_mode` in the same `suppress(OSError)`) rather than passing it bare.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/flowstate.py:_replace (≈line 211)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `stat.S_IMODE((tmp_path / "fresh.jsonl").stat().st_mode) == 0o644` hard-codes the result of `0o666 & ~umask` for the ambient umask 0o022, but the change's stated semantics for a brand-new file are "0666 & ~umask" (atomic_write), not a fixed 0644. The test never sets the process umask, so it is environment-dependent: run with umask 002 (common on group-shared checkouts) and the new file is created 0o664; run with umask 077 (common on security-hardened/CI hosts) and it is 0o600. In both cases this assertion fails while the code under test is behaving exactly as specified. To pin the intended behavior the test should compute the expectation from the current umask (e.g. `0o666 & ~os.umask(0)` round-tripped, or assert `mode == 0o666 & ~cur`), rather than comparing against the literal 0o644.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard collapses every non-ENOENT parent failure into `FileNotFoundError`. `Path.is_dir()` swallows `ENOTDIR`/`ELOOP` and returns `False`, so for a path whose parent component is a regular file, e.g. `/tmp/p.txt` exists as a file and you call `replace_text("/tmp/p.txt/child", "x")`, `named.is_symlink()` is `False`, `target.parent.is_dir()` returns `False` (ENOTDIR is ignored by pathlib), and the function raises `FileNotFoundError(ENOENT, ..., "/tmp/p.txt/child")`. `Path("/tmp/p.txt/child").write_text("x", "utf-8")` raises `NotADirectoryError(ENOTDIR)` instead. The same happens for an intermediate self-loop symlink: `/tmp/loopdir/child` where `loopdir -> loopdir` yields `FileNotFoundError` here but `ELOOP` from `write_text` (the loop check at the top only runs when the *final* component is a symlink, i.e. only after the `named.is_symlink()` branch is taken). The docstring advertises a drop-in for `write_text`, so callers that branch on `errno`/exception class now see a "missing file" where the path is actually misconfigured.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/fsio.py:replace_text (`if not target.parent.is_dir()` guard)

chunk_findings.detail: `replace_text` is not equivalent to `write_text` when the containing directory is not writable but the target file itself is — a case `write_text` handles fine. Given a directory `/d` with mode `0555` and an existing file `/d/f` mode `0644` owned by the caller, `Path("/d/f").write_text("x", "utf-8")` succeeds because it only truncates the existing inode in place (needs write permission on the file, not on the directory). `replace_text("/d/f", "x")` calls `atomic_write`, which must create a temporary file in `/d` and `os.replace` it into place, so it fails with `PermissionError`. This is exactly the situation for read-only package/config directories holding user-writable files, and the diff moves 21 `write_text` sites (including `DDFLOW.md` in `ddflow/api/rules.py`) onto `replace_text`, so the claim "Behaviour otherwise identical" does not hold for those callers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/fsio.py:replace_text (atomicity vs. `write_text`)

chunk_findings.detail: `replace_text` implements the write as `mkstemp` in the target's directory followed by `os.replace` over the target (the intent states this explicitly, and `flowstate._replace` is migrated to the same `atomic_write` primitive). `Path.write_text` instead opens the target for truncation and writes in place, keeping the same inode and never touching the parent directory entry. That equivalence breaks whenever the target is a mount point: `os.replace` onto a path that is a single-file bind mount returns `OSError: [Errno 16] Device or resource busy` (EBUSY), whereas `write_text` succeeds by writing through the mount into the file's contents. This is a first-class scenario for exactly the files adopt writes — the module's own comment at line ~638 notes it runs "inside a container", and bind-mounting an individual file such as `.ddflow/config.toml`, `.ddflow/.gitignore`, or the `.mcp.json`-style config handled at line 1215 (a very common docker-compose pattern, and the reason editors' "atomic save" is known to fail on bind-mounted files) now aborts the adopt/config-registration step with EBUSY instead of writing the file. The same regression occurs for the more general case where the target file is writable but its parent directory is not (atomic replace needs write permission on the directory to create the temp file; `write_text` only needs it on the file), e.g. a writable rule file inside a read-only vendored directory, including the symlink-through case this helper is documented to support when the link target lives in such a directory. `tests/test_fsio.py` compares only plain existing/missing regular files, so it will not exercise either environment.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py:636 (replace_text / atomic_write call sites)

chunk_findings.detail:
The assertion
`assert stat.S_IMODE((tmp_path / "fresh.jsonl").stat().st_mode) == 0o644`
hardcodes the default file mode as if it were a constant. The contract the change itself states is "new 0666&~umask" (and `FS._replace` now passes `mode=_mode(path)`, which for a non-existent path yields the `atomic_write` default). `0o644` is only what `0666 & ~umask` produces for `umask == 022`. On a machine (or CI image) with `umask 002` the freshly written `fresh.jsonl` gets mode `0o664`, and with `umask 077` it gets `0o600`; in both cases this assertion fails even though `_replace` is behaving exactly per spec. The expected value should be computed as `0o666 & ~current_umask` (e.g. by reading `os.umask` around the call or by comparing against a `Path.write_text`-created sibling), not written as a literal.

chunk_findings.detail: The new heading is an absolute claim that the full suite is executed exactly once per item, but the surrounding text (and the stated design) makes it run twice in every fallback case where the item's pipeline also has a `ci` gate. The same paragraph says "Everything else runs the whole suite in `unit_tests`" for a phase, a promotion, a larger task, `gates.unit_tests_scope = "full"`, "no base", "git cannot say what changed", "no test reaches the change", or "a command that does not run pytest", and the preceding sentence says the `ci` gate runs the whole suite on the merge result. So for, say, a task with 200 changed lines in a pipeline containing a `ci` gate, `unit_tests` runs the entire suite and then `ci` runs the entire suite again — two full runs for one item, directly contradicting the "runs once per item" claim (the same holds for the "no base" fallback, which is a common case). The claim should be scoped to items whose selection is actually taken (bug fixes/small tasks with a `ci` gate), or the sentence removed; as written the changed README misstates the cost model it is introducing.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten module docstring states the exception unconditionally: "for a bug fix or a small task whose pipeline has a `ci` gate, the unit_tests gate runs the selection and the ci gate runs the whole suite once, on the merge result; for anything else the unit_tests gate runs it." The behavior described in the change's own intent is narrower: the selection is used only once the `ci` gate is *recorded PASSED with the source_tree the worktree holds now*, and only when a selection can actually be made (base exists, git can answer, some test reaches the change, command is pytest). It also requires the task to be *small* (`changed_lines < [gates].unit_tests_small_lines`, default 150), not merely "a small task" by any definition. Concretely: a pipeline that *has* a `ci` gate whose outcome is skipped/failed/unavailable, or that passed on a different tree, or a bug fix with no git base, is documented here as running "the selection", while the gate actually runs the whole suite — exactly the "selection resting on a ci that never passed" confusion this change claims to have fixed (5ddf11f7). A reader trusting this docstring would expect a targeted run where a full run happens.

chunk_findings.detail: The bullet now asserts flatly that the full suite runs "once before the merge", but the paragraph it was rewritten to match describes exactly the cases where that is false. The same bullet says: "Once ci has passed on the tree as it is, a bug fix or a small task runs only the selection there ...; anything else, or an edit after ci, runs the whole suite." So for a phase item, a promotion, any task whose changed-lines-since-base is >= `[gates].unit_tests_small_lines` (150), a task with `[gates].unit_tests_scope=full`, or any item whose ci outcome is missing/skipped/unavailable/passed-on-other-source, the *whole* suite runs at the `ci` gate and then runs *again* at the `unit_tests` gate — both before the merge. Concretely: a 200-line task with a passing ci runs the full suite at `ddflow gate run <ID> ci` and then, because 200 >= 150, runs the full suite a second time at `ddflow gate run <ID> unit_tests`. The heading's "once" is therefore wrong for every fallback branch the change itself introduces; a developer reading the heading (and the "Then `ddflow gate run <ID> unit_tests`" instruction below it) is told the suite has already done its one full pass, which is not what the gate will do in those cases.

chunk_findings.detail: The change moves the enum entries for `dedupe.on_match`, the seven `enforce.*` knobs, `ci.on_merge` and `export.refresh` out of the explicit dict literal and into the leading `**_DC` spread (`KNOB_CHOICES: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]] = { **_DC, ... }`, line ~557). Because Python dicts preserve insertion order, those ten keys no longer appear at their old middle/end positions; they now appear at whatever position `declared_tables()` returns them, i.e. before all of the remaining explicit keys (`review.on_exceed`, `upgrade.skew`, `mcp.tools`, …). Concretely, `list(KNOB_CHOICES)` before the change read `[..., "schedule.parallel", "dedupe.on_match", "enforce.commit_without_lease", …, "ci.on_merge", "export.refresh"]`, and after the change those ten keys are hoisted to the front; the same is true of `KNOB_STRICTEST` if it is likewise built from `**_DS`. This directly contradicts the stated invariant that `KNOB_CHOICES`/`KNOB_STRICTEST`/`KNOB_OUTWARD` are "byte-identical before and after; only `KNOB_DOCS`' insertion order changes (read by key only)" — an order-insensitive `==` would not need that carve-out for `KNOB_DOCS`, and any consumer that serializes or iterates these tables in insertion order (e.g. `json.dumps(KNOB_CHOICES)` without `sort_keys`, or a README/`config` table rendered from the dict) now emits different bytes. If the pinned comparison is order-sensitive, this refactor breaks the pin it claims to preserve; the fix is to keep the legacy keys' relative order (or make all consumers explicitly order-insensitive/sorted, matching how `KNOB_DOCS` is described).

chunk_findings.detail: `isinstance(v, int | float)` is a *runtime* expression, and the `X | Y` union form is only accepted by `isinstance` on Python 3.10+ (`type.__or__` / `types.UnionType` were added in 3.10). `from __future__ import annotations` at the top of the file does **not** help here — it only affects annotation syntax, not an `isinstance` call executed at runtime. On an interpreter older than 3.10 (which is exactly the scenario the `from __future__ import annotations` idiom in this module is there to support), evaluating `isinstance(v, int | float)` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'type'` before the comparison even runs. So given a `[dedupe]` config that carries a similarity-bound value (`check=` invoked), the environment `<3.10` makes this check crash the config load instead of returning `"must be a number between 0 and 1"`, breaking the "value checks moved *verbatim*" / behaviour-preserving guarantee. The previous form is `isinstance(v, (int, float))`, which is version-independent.

titles: ddflow/config.py — `KNOB_CHOICES` (and the same construction pattern for `KNOB_STRICTEST`)

chunk_findings.detail: The moved knobs (`dedupe.on_match`, the seven `enforce.*`, `ci.on_merge`, `export.refresh`) were previously only present as literal entries in the tail of `KNOB_CHOICES`/`KNOB_STRICTEST`. After this change they are supplied by `**_DC`/`**_DS`, i.e. prepended from `declared_tables()`, and the literal entries are deleted. The construction is order-preserving (`{**declared, <literal>}`), so the insertion order of `KNOB_CHOICES` and `KNOB_STRICTEST` necessarily changes too — the moved keys now occupy positions dictated by section/field-declaration order rather than their old slots between `schedule.parallel` and `review.on_exceed`. The stated invariant "only KNOB_DOCS' insertion order changes (read by key only)" is therefore false for these two tables (and any moved knob that also had an `OUTWARD` entry). Concretely, any order-sensitive pin/consumer — e.g. a `--json`/`--explain` dump that iterates the table, a `repr`/`json.dumps` snapshot, or a README/knob-table generator walking the dict in iteration order — will now emit these knobs in different positions and will not be byte-identical to the pre-change output, contradicting the pinned guarantee. chunk_findings.detail: `isinstance(v, int | float)` evaluates the union `int | float` at runtime. `types.UnionType` is only accepted by `isinstance` on Python 3.10+, whereas the module (like the rest of the package) still opens with `from __future__ import annotations`, i.e. annotations are kept lazy precisely so the code runs on interpreters older than 3.10. On such an interpreter, `int | float` raises `TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for |: 'type' and 'type'`, so validating the dedupe similarity knob (e.g. `similarity = 0.5` in `[dedupe]`) crashes instead of returning the `"must be a number between 0 and 1"` message that the pre-refactor `(int, float)` form produced. The equivalent-version-safe form is `isinstance(v, (int, float))`.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor claims docs are carried verbatim and that `ddflow config --explain` (text and `--json`) stays byte-identical, but the section class docstring is not carried verbatim: the original was the single line `` `[ids]`: the template each record kind's id is minted from.`` and the new one appends a second paragraph ("Each template is checked by `id_template_problem`: ids are file names, branch names and glob tokens ... refused by the write paths."). These `` `[section]`: ... `` class docstrings are the per-section help text that `config --explain` renders as the section header, so running `ddflow config --explain` (or `--json`) on the `[ids]` section now emits those extra lines where before it emitted only the one-line description. That is exactly the pinned text the change is supposed to keep byte-identical; the added paragraph should have been dropped (the `_RULES`/per-kind knob docs already cover the check semantics). Demonstrated input: `ddflow config --explain` before vs. after the change — the `[ids]` header gains two sentences, so any byte-for-byte comparison of the explain output fails.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/ids.py IdsConfig (class docstring)

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces the old eagerly-bound `functools.partial(id_template_problem, kind)` comprehension with a `lambda v: id_template_problem(kind, v)` created once per id kind. Because the lambda is created inside the same comprehension/loop scope where `kind` is the single loop variable, every lambda closes over the *same* cell, not over the value of `kind` at creation time. After the comprehension finishes, `kind` holds the last iterated kind, so all per-kind checks call `id_template_problem(<last-kind>, v)`. Concretely: a template such as `"{lastkind_id}"` supplied for an earlier kind (e.g. a template using the previous kind's placeholder) will be checked against the last kind's rules and wrongly accepted, and a template correctly using the field's own placeholder will be wrongly rejected. `functools.partial` bound the kind eagerly, so the old code checked each field against its own kind; the new code does not. This is exactly the classic late-binding closure bug and it is a behaviour change, not a behaviour-preserving refactor. Fix by binding eagerly, e.g. `check=(lambda k: lambda v: id_template_problem(k, v))(kind)` or `functools.partial(id_template_problem, kind)` as before.

chunk_findings.detail: The intent states the per-field template checks were rewritten from "a functools.partial comprehension" to `check=lambda v: id_template_problem(kind, v) per field`. If, as that description implies, these knobs are produced by a loop/comprehension over the id kinds (which is the only way the original could have been a `functools.partial` comprehension), then every lambda captures the same closure cell for `kind`, and by the time any check runs `kind` holds the *last* iterated value. `functools.partial(id_template_problem, kind)` bound its kind eagerly, so this is a behavioural regression, not a preservation. Concretely: with kinds `("task", "phase", "target")` where `target` is the last kind, a value written to the `task` knob that is invalid for `task` but valid for `target` (e.g. a template using a token only `target` permits) will satisfy `id_template_problem("target", v)` and pass validation it should have failed — the same wrong check is applied to every field. Fix by binding eagerly, e.g. `check=lambda v, k=kind: id_template_problem(k, v)` or `functools.partial(id_template_problem, kind)`.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_lint_outcome` returns `O.refused(op, str(exc))` for `ManifestError` *unconditionally*, i.e. it never consults `policy`. Every other return path respects the policy (`"off"` → `None`; `"warn"` → `O.ok(..., warning=...)`; only `"block"` → `O.refused`). But `version_cut` decides whether to abort purely on the exit status:

```python
blocked = _lint_outcome("version.cut", repo, cfg)
if blocked is not None and blocked.exit != 0:
    return blocked
```

So with a non-blocking policy the release is still hard-blocked whenever the lint cannot run. Concrete input: a checkout of the ddflow tree whose `upgrade_manifest.toml` is malformed, and `[release] manifest_lint = "warn"` (or the operator running `version_lint --waive X --reason ...` under `manifest_lint = "off"`, since `_lint_outcome` proceeds when `waive` is set). `UM.lint()` raises `ManifestError`, the `except` at line 167 returns `O.refused` with a non-zero exit, and `version_cut` returns exit 3 instead of emitting the warning it promised. This contradicts the documented/configured behavior — under `warn`/`off` an unparseable manifest should at most produce a warning, not abort the cut — and it also means the "fail" signal for `warn` is indistinguishable from a real `block`. Either the `except` needs to be policy-aware (warn/off → `O.ok` with the error text as `warning`, or `None` under `off`), or the `block`-only exit-3 contract in the docstring is wrong.

chunk_findings.detail: `waive()` records `Waiver(hits[0].id, " ".join(reason.split()))` with `version` left at its `""` default, and `lint()` decides coverage only by `u.id in by_change`, where `by_change` is keyed by `w.change`; `Waiver.version` is parsed by `load_waivers()` but never written and never consulted. Waivers are therefore permanent, not "for this release" as `report()` tells the operator ("Waive a change for this release: ..."). Concretely: suppose the default of knob `foo` changes 1 -> 2 in release 1.2 and the operator runs `... version lint --waive knob_changed:foo --reason "..."`, which appends `[[waiver]] change = "knob_changed:foo"` to `waivers.toml`. At 1.2's cut the manifest now replays `foo = 2`. In release 1.3 the default changes again, 2 -> 3. `lint()` builds `Unmanifested("knob_changed", "foo", old=2, new=3)`, whose `id` is exactly `"knob_changed:foo"`, so the stale waiver swallows it into `out.waived` and, under the default `block` policy, the 1.3 change ships unannounced with no prompt — the same change-id match is the only key, so a waiver for one value transition silently covers every later transition of that knob. If waivers are meant to be one-shot (as the data model's `version` field and the "for this release" wording imply), `waive()` must record the version and `lint()` must filter `by_change` by it (e.g. only waivers for the current release / empty version), which it does not.

chunk_findings.detail: The lint is invoked from the publish job, whose checkout is shallow: the step immediately above it (context lines `with:` / `ref: ${{ needs.gate.outputs.sha }}`) passes only `ref`, so `actions/checkout` uses its default `fetch-depth: 1` and no tag refs are fetched. Identifying "the unmanifested changes" (the knob defaults / event kinds that changed since the previous release and are not covered by an entry in `ddflow/templates/upgrade/`) requires that previous release's state — i.e. the previous release tag and its tree. In this environment, `git describe --tags --abbrev=0`, `git diff <prev-tag>..HEAD` or `git show <prev-tag>:...` all fail with "unknown revision"/"no tag found" because neither the tag nor its commits exist in the depth-1 clone. The result is either a hard error that fails the publish job for every release that touches a knob, or, if the lint swallows the missing baseline, a lint that sees only the working tree and therefore silently reports nothing in CI while passing locally in `scripts/release.sh` (which runs on a full clone) — the guard is exactly the place it is supposed to work (the tag-triggered release) and it is defeated there. Adding `fetch-depth: 0` (or fetching the previous tag explicitly) to this job's checkout is required for the new step to be able to do the comparison the intent describes.

chunk_findings.detail: The new paragraph tells the operator, at a blocking lint, to change the policy with `ddflow config release.manifest_lint warn|off`. That is not the editing form this same README documents. Twenty lines earlier in the very same knob/config section it states: "`ddflow config --set <key> <value>` edits one key in place, preserving comments" — i.e. the documented write form is `ddflow config --set <key> <value>`, and a bare `ddflow config <key>` (no `--set`) is at best a read. An operator who hits the exit-3 block and follows option (3) literally runs `ddflow config release.manifest_lint warn`, which does not perform the in-place write the text promises; the policy stays `block` and the release stays stopped. The two forms cannot both be the write path as documented, so one of them (this new line, since it is the one introduced by the change) is wrong; it should be `ddflow config --set release.manifest_lint warn` (or `off`).

chunk_findings.detail: The docstring says the lint must no-op when "``repo`` is not the tree that ships the manifest (a project's own releases are not ddflow's)", but the check does not test whether `repo` is ddflow's source tree — it only tests whether the *imported* package's manifest file happens to live somewhere under `repo` after `resolve()`. When ddflow is installed into a virtualenv inside an unrelated project (the normal result of `uv run`/`uv sync`/`pip install` into `./.venv`), `UM.MANIFEST.resolve()` is `<project>/.venv/lib/python3.x/site-packages/ddflow/templates/upgrade`, and `Path.is_relative_to(<project>)` is True, so the guard passes instead of returning `None`. `UM.lint()` then compares that installed ddflow's `knob_defaults()`/`event_kinds()` with its own shipped manifest; if the install is a dev/unreleased build that added a knob or event kind without a matching `ddflow/templates/upgrade/` entry, `res.clean` is False and, with the default `cfg.release.manifest_lint == "block"`, `version_cut` returns `O.refused("version.cut", …)` (exit 3) and refuses the *user's* release, printing ddflow's unmanifested changes. Concrete input: project P with `P/.venv` containing `pip install git+…/ddflow@main`; running `ddflow version cut` in P is refused even though P ships no upgrade manifest. The check should identify the source tree (e.g. `(repo / "ddflow" / "templates" / "upgrade").is_dir()`, or that `repo` is the package's source root), not where the package happens to be installed.

chunk_findings.detail: For a knob that was removed from the schema (`kind == "knob_removed"`) the item's action is chosen with `OPERATOR if operator_set else ...`, and `operator_set = cfg.sources.get(key, "default") != "default"`. But a knob that no longer exists in the schema is, by definition, not a known knob, so it has no source entry — the file itself establishes that "the project carried/set this removed knob" is signalled by `cfg.unknown_knobs` (the guard `if kind == "knob_removed" and key not in cfg.unknown_knobs: continue`, comment "the project never carried it"). So every removed-knob item that survives the guard still has `operator_set == False`: its `set_by` is `""` even though the summary asserts "this project's config still sets it", and its action is `agent`. Concretely: the manifest records `knob_removed "log.dedupe"` at 0.2.0, and the project (baseline 0.1.3) has `log.dedupe = false` written in a config layer, so `log.dedupe` is in `cfg.unknown_knobs` but not in `cfg.sources`. The plan marks the item `agent`, so `ddflow upgrade --apply` removes the operator's explicit value without the `--confirm log.dedupe --reason` that D-upgrade-config-changes requires (and the failing-first case "an operator-set knob whose default/name changed is refused without --confirm" — a rename produces exactly such a removed old key — would not be refused).

chunk_findings.detail: `_net` collapses "added then changed" and "changed back", but not "removed then added": when the change sequence for one key is `knob_removed` (0.2.0) followed by `knob_added` (0.3.0), the `prev[0] == "knob_removed"` branch rewrites the entry as `("knob_added", c, c.old, c.new)`. A knobs first event since baseline being a removal proves the knob already existed before the baseline, so the correct net for that sequence is "no change" (or a default change), not an addition. Input: a project at baseline 0.1.3 that never set `log.dedupe`, with a manifest that removes `log.dedupe` in 0.2.0 and re-adds it in 0.3.0. `config_items` then emits `kind == "knob_added"`, summary "new knob log.dedupe (default ...)", action `note`, even though the project already had the knob before 0.1.3; the false item also makes `total > 0`, so `up_to_date` is false and the CLI/MCP report a pending plan (and a non-zero "plan pending" exit) for a project with nothing to do.

chunk_findings.detail: `_net` overwrites a knob's history when it sees a removal, losing the information that the knob was *added* inside the window, and then treats a subsequent re-add as a changed default. Concretely, for a project whose baseline is before all of these, and a manifest whose changes since baseline are `knob_added K = 1`, then `knob_removed K`, then `knob_added K = 1` (a knob that existed for one release and was reintroduced with the same default), the loop does: step 2 stores `("knob_removed", c, 1, None)`, step 3 hits `elif prev is not None and prev[0] == "knob_removed"` and stores `("knob_changed", c, 1, 1)`. The final comprehension then drops it (`v[0] == "knob_changed" and v[2] == v[3]`), so `config_items` never emits the new knob at all — even though the knob is brand new for this project and the module docstring promises "Added then changed is an addition with the last default" / a new knob is a `note` item. With a different reintroduced default (say `1` then `2`) the same branch instead emits `change: "knob_changed"` with summary `default of K changed 1 -> 2` and, because the project never set it, `action: "agent"` (with `--apply` as the fix) rather than the `note` a newly-added knob should get; and if the project *does* set `K` (so `cfg.sources` has it and `operator_set` is true), it emits `action: "needs operator confirmation"` requiring `--confirm`, whereas the decision says "a knob added that the project already sets needs nothing and is left out". The branch's own comment ("its removal is the first thing that happened to it") shows it only considers the removal-first case; it must distinguish a removal whose predecessor was an `knob_added` inside the window from one for a knob that predates the baseline.

chunk_findings.detail: The tool advertises the contract "Dry run (the default). false is refused: no apply mode yet.", but the lambda `plan=a.get("plan", True) is not False` does not refuse an explicit `false`; it evaluates to `False` and forwards it as `plan=False` into `_api().upgrade(...)`, i.e. the non-dry-run/apply path. The declared default for the property is also `False`, contradicting the description that the default is a dry run. Concrete scenario: an MCP client sends `{"plan": false}` (or, if the framework materialises the declared `False` default for an omitted argument, sends nothing at all); the call becomes `upgrade(repo, plan=False, agent=...)` rather than the documented refusal/dry-run. Since `ddflow_upgrade`'s property list contains no `confirm`/`reason` arguments, this path also cannot supply the confirmation that operator decision D-upgrade-config-changes requires before any operator-set knob is changed, and it breaks the "writes nothing" guarantee for a call the schema presents as default. Either the lambda must hard-refuse `false` (e.g. always pass `plan=True`) or the property default/description must be corrected; as written, the documented refusal is not implemented at this boundary.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier triage confirmed that `knob_removed` followed by `knob_added` must become a `knob_changed`, and the new branch does that with `out[c.key] = ("knob_changed", c, prev[2], c.new)`. But `prev[2]` is *not* the baseline value whenever a `knob_changed` for the same key preceded the removal: the removal branch unconditionally overwrites the entry with `("knob_removed", c, c.old, None)`, discarding the baseline `old` that the first `knob_changed` had captured, and the re-add then takes `prev[2] == c.old`, i.e. the default as it stood at removal time (a value the project, sitting at `baseline`, never applied). Concretely, with a project at baseline where `dedupe.window` default is 5 and manifest changes `knob_changed 5->7` (0.1.5), `knob_removed old=7` (0.2.0), `knob_added new=7` (0.3.0), `_net` yields `("knob_changed", c3, old=7, new=7)`; the final comprehension `{k: v for k, v in out.items() if not (v[0] == "knob_changed" and v[2] == v[3])}` then *drops the key entirely*. So the plan emits no config item and can report `up_to_date: true` (exit 0) even though the effective shipped default for this project went 5 -> 7 — exactly the "changed defaults are always listed" guarantee of D-upgrade-config-changes is violated, and an operator relying on the plan never learns the project's behavior changed. (In the milder intermediate case where the values differ, the item is listed but its summary advertises the wrong `old`, e.g. "changed 6 -> 7" when the project actually held 5.) The confirmation probe only covers a bare removed-then-added sequence, so it does not exercise this path; the fix is to keep the first captured baseline `old` when rewriting a removal into a change (and to only fall back to `c.old` when no prior entry exists).

chunk_findings.detail: The fix removes `json`, `limit` and `reason` from the properties map that `_schema` returns, but that returned schema is the one carrying `additionalProperties: false` — the exact gate Bf84a50bce3 names ("rejected ... as unknown arguments (additionalProperties false)"). Because the change does not relax `additionalProperties` (nor keep the property with a marker), the schema now positively *forbids* the very arguments the change claims to accept: any `tools/call` that still sends them (the only callers this alias exists for) fails argument validation against this schema before execution ever reaches the stripping code at lines 660-664, so `args` is never sanitized and the `retired` set at line 661 is never built. The deprecation note at line 767 therefore is unreachable for these arguments as well. Concretely: `ddflow_rule_list` with `{"json": true}` (or `ddflow_rule_list` with `{"limit": 5}`, or `ddflow_rule_remove` with `{"reason": "x"}`) still returns the additional-properties rejection rather than a result plus the one deprecation note, so the stated promise in the comment above the change ("A deprecated argument is still ACCEPTED") is not kept. To accept a deprecated argument while not advertising it, the argument must remain valid under the schema used for validation (keep the property, or make `additionalProperties` permissive) and be hidden only from the `tools/list` representation; dropping it from the schema that rejects unknown arguments guarantees the bug persists.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:128-131 (`_schema`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to prove the deprecated `limit` argument is a no-op — its docstring says the arguments are "ignored" and it asserts `old["content"][0] == plain["content"][0]` as "the answer is the same without them". But the fixture only creates a single rule (`run_cli(repo, "rule", "add", "--id", "r-one", ...)`), so `limit=5` cannot distinguish an ignored limit from a honoured one: any implementation that filters to `limit` rules returns the same one-rule list either way. The assertion is therefore vacuous for `limit` and would pass unchanged even if the fix accidentally re-implemented `limit` (e.g. slicing the result to 5 entries), which is exactly the behaviour D-compat's no-op rule forbids. A non-vacuous input would be `limit=0` (a limit-honouring implementation returns an empty list, differing from `plain`) or more than five rules with `limit=5`. The `json` half of the comparison is meaningful only if the default output is non-JSON, so the "same answer" claim rests on an unverified default as well.

data.body:
--apply <category,...>|all. Before ANY write: snapshot every file it will touch to .ddflow/backups/<ts>-<from>-to-<to>/ (local, git-ignored) and print the git diff command; driver docs and rules blocks get a version+body-sha256 header (like export docs) so hand edits are detected and the file is moved aside (.local-edits) or refused, never silently overwritten (also fix adopt --refresh-docs to use it). Dangling git-hook binary is repaired by hooks install. Idempotent: second apply is a no-op. Appends upgrade.applied (from, to, categories, backup) so replay explains it. Config-default changes are never auto-applied: they are listed with 'pin old behaviour: ddflow config --set X old' and recorded when the operator acknowledges.
Failing-first: local edit in driver doc survives to .local-edits and is reported; apply twice = identical tree; kill mid-apply leaves backup and a re-runnable plan; replay shows the upgrade event.

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-backups (2026-10-03): backups are LOCAL by default ([upgrade].backup = local|snapshot|none, default local, .ddflow/backups git-ignored, [upgrade].backup_keep); a git-tracked snapshot is the opt-in (--snapshot or [upgrade].backup = snapshot; refused clearly on a dirty tree or without git); `ddflow upgrade --restore <backup>`; configurable via config, CLI and MCP. README MUST explain both options, the default, what each costs and how to restore (acceptance: a test asserts the README section exists and names both).

OPERATOR DECISION D-upgrade-config-changes (2026-10-03): agents may apply upgrade config changes where the project never set the value; any value the operator set (present in any config layer, env, or set via ddflow config/ddflow_configure) is never changed without the operator's confirmation: the plan marks it 'needs operator confirmation', --apply refuses it unless --confirm <knob> --reason is passed and is recorded; changed shipped defaults are always listed in the plan, notice and upgrade.applied. [upgrade].config_changes = agent|ask|operator (default agent). Failing-first test: an operator-set knob whose default/name changed is refused without --confirm, applied with it; an unset knob is applied by the agent; both appear in the plan.

D-compat (operator 2026-10-06): part of P-unify's finish line (B-uni-acceptance needs it); P-unify's breaking changes are applied through it (B-uni-compat-migrations).

Split into: B-upgrade.4-apply.1-core, B-upgrade.4-apply.2-docs, B-upgrade.4-apply.3-snapshot.

chunk_findings.detail: The payload builds each entry with hard indexing of all four fields: `{k: i[k] for k in ("key", "change", "old", "new")}` for every config item whose id is in `ok`. But this file only ever guarantees `old`/`new` for `kind == "knob_changed"`: `_apply_config` guards the only read of `item['old']` behind `if kind == "knob_changed"`, and the `knob_removed` branch never reads `item['new']` at all. Concrete input: the "new knob" note the module docstring explicitly describes (a config item with `change` = `knob_added`, `action` = NOTE). `_select` sends it to `todo` (`cat == "config"` is in `_VERSIONED`, so the NOTE-skip branch does not fire; `_needs_confirmation` is False because the action is neither OPERATOR nor AGENT), `_apply_config` returns ACKNOWLEDGED, so it lands in `ok`, and then the comprehension evaluates `i["old"]` → `KeyError: 'old'`. Because that dict is evaluated as the argument of `log.append(...)`, the exception escapes `apply()` after `_execute` has already rewritten the TOML and after `make_backup` has copied it: `ddflow upgrade --apply` dies with a traceback, no `upgrade.applied` event is ever appended (the recorded version never moves), and the next `upgrade --plan` re-lists the same item. The same happens for a `knob_removed` item, which has no `new` (it can reach `ok` either as an agent-level ACKNOWLEDGED item or as a confirmed OPERATOR item whose `_remove_key` returned True) — again crashing after the write.

chunk_findings.detail: `counts = {s: sum(1 for r in results if r["status"] == s) for s in (REFUSED, FAILED)}` and `exit_code = 1 if counts[FAILED] else (3 if counts[REFUSED] else 0)` mean the `UNAVAILABLE` status is invisible to the exit code, even though `_finish`'s own contract says "exit is 0 when everything chosen was applied, acknowledged or already fine, 1 when an applier failed". Concrete input: a project with a repair item whose tool is absent, run as `ddflow upgrade --apply --categories repairs`; `_run_repairs` produces `_rec(i, UNAVAILABLE, f"could not run: {r['unavailable']}")`, nothing is applied or acknowledged, yet the command prints `[unavailable] <repair>: could not run: ...` and exits 0. CI/scripts gating on the exit status treat the requested repair as successfully performed when it silently never ran; `UNAVAILABLE` is likewise excluded from `changed`, so the `applied` count under-reports what actually happened.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_run_repairs` records an item whose `RP.apply` record carries `unavailable` with status `UNAVAILABLE` ("could not run: ..."), but `_finish` computes the exit code only from `REFUSED` and `FAILED`:

    counts = {s: sum(1 for r in results if r["status"] == s) for s in (REFUSED, FAILED)}
    exit_code = 1 if counts[FAILED] else (3 if counts[REFUSED] else 0)

so an `UNAVAILABLE` item contributes neither to `failed` nor to the exit code, and the command exits 0. The module docstring defines `exit` as "0 when everything chosen was applied, acknowledged or already fine, 1 when an applier failed"; a repair that "could not run" is neither applied/acknowledged nor "already fine". Concrete input: a plan whose chosen `repairs` item is passed to `RP.apply`, which returns a record with `unavailable` set (e.g. the repair's tooling/environment is missing). `_run_repairs` returns `[{"status": "unavailable", ...}]`, `_finish` reports `failed: 0`, `exit: 0`, so a CI script that checks the exit code treats the skipped repair as success even though nothing was repaired.
```

Everything else I checked holds up: the `_unresolved`/`new_to` version logic moves the version only when every `config`/`features` item is in the settled set, `touched` matches the files the config/hook/mcp/instruction appliers write, the backup is taken before any write and short-circuits (`OSError` → nothing changed), and the event is appended only when something settled. I am not confident enough in any other suspected issue (e.g. backup-directory name collisions depend on `clock.compact_at()` granularity, which isn't in this diff) to report it.

chunk_findings.detail: On a partial apply the recorded event contradicts itself. `new_to` is computed as `(frm or UNSTAMPED) if _unresolved(...) else to`, and the event stores `"to": new_to`, but the human-readable `"summary"` is built with the raw running version: `f"upgrade {frm or 'unstamped'} -> {to}: {', '.join(done_cats)}"`. Run e.g. `ddflow upgrade --apply --categories config` on a project stamped `1.0` where `features` items are still pending: the appended event has `"from": "1.0"`, `"to": "1.0"` (correctly, the version did not move) yet `"summary": "upgrade 1.0 -> 2.0: config"`, i.e. it claims the upgrade reached the running version. Any replay/`explain` consumer reading `summary` gets the wrong target version. The summary should use `new_to`.

chunk_findings.detail: `dest.mkdir(parents=True)` is called without `exist_ok=True`, and the directory name depends only on `backup_name(frm, to)` (timestamp + from + to), not on the item set. So any two applies that share the same `from`/`to` and fall in the same timestamp bucket collide. Concretely, running `ddflow upgrade --apply --categories config` and then `ddflow upgrade --apply --categories hooks` (same plan, same `project_version`/`running`) within the same clock tick makes the second call raise `FileExistsError`; it is caught by the `except OSError` in `apply`, which then reports "no backup could be written (...); nothing was changed", marks every selected item `failed`, and exits 1 — the second apply does nothing at all even though there is no real failure. The backup dir needs a uniqueness guard (`exist_ok=True` plus a suffix, or cleaning/mkdir on a fresh stamp).

chunk_findings.detail: The previous finding still holds. This diff part removes `NOT_YET` and rewrites the advertised fixes from `ddflow upgrade --apply (not available yet: this ddflow only plans)` to plain `ddflow upgrade --apply` (upgrade_plan.py lines ~157-162 and ~199-203), which is only coherent if the apply path is now live and its exit code is meaningful. Nothing in the visible diff changes `_run_repairs`/`_finish`, so the reporting gap is only made more reachable: `_run_repairs` still records an item whose `RP.apply` result carries `unavailable` with status `UNAVAILABLE` ("could not run: ..."), while `_finish` still computes `counts = {s: sum(1 for r in results if r["status"] == s) for s in (REFUSED, FAILED)}` and `exit_code = 1 if counts[FAILED] else (3 if counts[REFUSED] else 0)`. Given an upgrade where a repair is unrunnable (e.g. apply reports `unavailable` for a hooks/mcp repair that now carries the new `paths` key added in this diff), the item contributes to neither `REFUSED` nor `FAILED`, the command prints the fix `ddflow upgrade --apply` and exits 0, so a script/CI consuming the exit code sees success for a repair that never ran. The removal of `NOT_YET` (the only thing that previously signalled "this route is not implemented") means the advertised `--apply` invocation is now expected to report real outcomes, and the UNAVAILABLE case is silently swallowed. No probe or fix for this appears in this diff part, so it remains reportable.

chunk_findings.detail: On a partial apply the recorded event contradicts itself. `new_to` is computed as `(frm or UNSTAMPED) if _unresolved(...) else to`, and the event stores `"to": new_to`, but the human-readable `"summary"` is built with the raw running version: `f"upgrade {frm or 'unstamped'} -> {to}: {', '.join(done_cats)}"`. Run e.g. `ddflow upgrade --apply --categories config` on a project stamped `1.0` where `features` items are still pending: the appended event has `"from": "1.0"`, `"to": "1.0"` (correctly, the version did not move) yet `"summary": "upgrade 1.0 -> 2.0: config"`, i.e. it claims the upgrade reached the running version. Any replay/`explain` consumer reading `summary` gets the wrong target version. The summary should use `new_to`.

chunk_findings.detail: `dest.mkdir(parents=True)` is called without `exist_ok=True`, and the directory name depends only on `backup_name(frm, to)` (timestamp + from + to), not on the item set. So any two applies that share the same `from`/`to` and fall in the same timestamp bucket collide. Concretely, running `ddflow upgrade --apply --categories config` and then `ddflow upgrade --apply --categories hooks` (same plan, same `project_version`/`running`) within the same clock tick makes the second call raise `FileExistsError`; it is caught by the `except OSError` in `apply`, which then reports "no backup could be written (...); nothing was changed", marks every selected item `failed`, and exits 1 — the second apply does nothing at all even though there is no real failure. The backup dir needs a uniqueness guard (`exist_ok=True` plus a suffix, or cleaning/mkdir on a fresh stamp).

chunk_findings.detail: `refused` is built as `[a for a in actions if isinstance(a, Refused)]`, i.e. it is a list of `Refused` *action/data objects* (the type is imported from `..services.adopt` and used as an `isinstance` target on the elements of `actions`). `str.join` only accepts actual `str` instances — it does not call `__str__` on its arguments. So for the exact input this change is written to handle (a MANAGED_MARK/BEGIN-END doc under the docs dir that was written by a newer ddflow, making `refresh_docs` append a `Refused` marker to `actions`), the line raises `TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, Refused found` instead of returning the intended exit-3 refusal. The message must be materialized, e.g. `"; ".join(str(a) for a in refused)` (or from a `.message`/`.reason` field on `Refused`), and the code is only correct if `Refused` happens to subclass `str`, which the `isinstance(a, Refused)`-on-actions usage does not imply.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py (the `O.refused("setup", "; ".join(refused), **data)` line in `setup`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_backup_docs` builds the backup set as `driver_drift(...)` plus every `rules_status(...)` entry whose `needs_attention` flag is set:

```python
stale += [r.path for r in rules_status(repo, docs_dir=docs_dir) if r.needs_attention]
files = [Path(repo) / rel for rel in dict.fromkeys(stale) if only is None or rel in only]
```

But `rules_status` also emits `RulesState(name, MISSING)` (unchanged context in hunk `@@ -434,11 +483,7 @@`) for every entry of `RULES_FILES` that does not exist on disk, and the path stored for such an entry is `name` — a *non-existent* repo-relative path. A missing rules file certainly `needs_attention`, so it lands in `stale`, and `files` then contains e.g. `<repo>/AGENTS.md` even though nothing is there. `make_backup(repo, files, ...)` is then asked to copy a source that does not exist; for a normal `shutil`-based copier this raises `FileNotFoundError` (it only stays silent if the helper happens to filter non-existent paths — which the docstring's "the documents a refresh is about to rewrite" does not suggest it does).

Concrete input: adopt a project, delete one of its rules files (`rm AGENTS.md`), then invoke the refresh path that now defaults to backing up (`backup=True`), e.g. `ddflow adopt --refresh-docs`. Before this change the missing file would simply be regenerated; after it, the backup step runs first on a path that isn't a file, so the refresh can fail instead of healing the repo. Even under a lenient `make_backup`, the function's stated contract ("the documents a refresh is about to rewrite", "the directory, or `""` when none differs") is violated, since a file that is going to be *created* is being treated as a stale document to copy aside.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/services/adopt.py::_backup_docs`

chunk_findings.detail: The new `owned` branch guards `replace_text` with `except NewerContent` and converts the failure into `Refused(...)`/`REFUSED ...`, but the `has_legacy_block(existing)` branch one line below calls `replace_text(path, head + section.strip() + tail)` with no such guard. The two branches write through the same I/O primitive, so the guard is only meaningful if `replace_text` can raise `NewerContent` — which the sibling branch asserts by catching it. Input: `ddflow adopt --refresh-docs` on a project whose doc still carries the legacy `LEGACY_BEGIN`/`LEGACY_END` markers and whose file has been edited since ddflow last wrote it. Result: the owned path returns `REFUSED ...` cleanly, while the legacy path lets `NewerContent` escape `_upsert_block`, aborting the adopt run with an unhandled exception instead of the intended refusal. Whichever behavior is correct, having both under the same call site is a defect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py `_upsert_block` (legacy branch)

chunk_findings.detail: A backed-up file whose project-relative path is exactly `manifest.json` collides with the backup manifest itself. For `f = <repo>/manifest.json`: `stored = f.relative_to(repo).as_posix() = "manifest.json"`, so the copy is written to `dest / "manifest.json"`. Immediately after the copy loop, `replace_text(dest / MANIFEST, json.dumps(manifest, ...))` writes to the same path (`MANIFEST = "manifest.json"`), silently overwriting the user's file with the manifest. The manifest entry still records `{"path": "manifest.json", "stored": "manifest.json", "existed": true}`, so a restore reading that entry gets the backup manifest rather than the original file, and the original content is gone. Any caller that passes a top-level `manifest.json` (e.g. `upgrade --apply` / `adopt --refresh-docs` on a project that contains one) loses that file's backup.

chunk_findings.detail: The second loop of `test_second_adopt_is_a_noop` iterates over *every* file produced by an adopt (`for rel in before:`) and claims to assert "has two managed blocks" for each. The old code counted the generic `BEGIN` constant, which (as shown by the other hunk at line ~112, where `text.index(BEGIN)` is used to locate the block in *arbitrary* non-AIDER rule files) matches a managed-block opener on any surface, so it counted blocks in every rule's file. The new code counts the rule-id-specific literal `"ddflow:begin rules/work-queue"`. For any file that does not belong to the `rules/work-queue` rule the string never occurs, so `count(...) == 0 <= 1` and the assertion passes unconditionally. Concrete case: if a regression makes adopt emit the managed block twice into, say, the aider/other FORM_BLOCK surface, this assertion still returns 0 and reports success, silently dropping the per-file duplicate-block check for every surface except work-queue (and if the real marker text differs even slightly — e.g. a different separator or id — it drops it for work-queue too, becoming entirely vacuous). The check should be derived from `block_body`/the generic marker rather than a hard-coded single-rule string.

chunk_findings.detail: `refused` is a list of `Refused` instances (`[a for a in actions if isinstance(a, Refused)]`), but `str.join` requires actual `str` instances — it does not call `__str__`/`__format__` on its elements. Given the documented scenario in the adjacent comment ("A file a NEWER ddflow wrote is refused (exit 3, 'upgrade ddflow to >= X')"), any run of `adopt --refresh-docs` over a docs tree containing at least one `MANAGED_MARK` doc written by a newer ddflow makes `refresh_docs` return at least one `Refused` entry in `actions`. At that point `"; ".join(refused)` raises `TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, Refused found`, so the command crashes with a traceback instead of returning the intended exit-3 refused result. The expression needs the elements stringified (e.g. `"; ".join(str(a) for a in refused)`), or `Refused` would have to be a `str` subclass, which is inconsistent with it being used as a returned action object filtered by `isinstance` alongside the other (dict/object) actions.

chunk_findings.detail:
`block_body`'s legacy branch only tests membership of the two markers and never pairs them or checks order:

```python
if LEGACY_BEGIN in text and LEGACY_END in text:
    return text[text.index(LEGACY_BEGIN) + len(LEGACY_BEGIN) : text.index(LEGACY_END)]
```

For `text = "<!-- DDFLOW:END -->\nnotes\n<!-- DDFLOW:BEGIN (managed — edits inside this block are overwritten) -->"` (END above BEGIN — e.g. a user reordering sections, or an END left over from a prior block), `text.index(LEGACY_END)` is *before* `text.index(LEGACY_BEGIN) + len(LEGACY_BEGIN)`, so the slice is `""`. `block_body` then returns the empty string: not `None`, and not a `RegionError`, even though the docstring it was given states "Raises RegionError for broken markers." Worse, it disagrees with its sibling on the *same* input — `has_legacy_block(text)` returns `True` (it only checks the two substrings), so a migration/refresh path that guards on `has_legacy_block(...)` and then feeds `block_body(...)` onward hands an empty, falsy "old body" to the writer (and an empty replacement target in a `str.replace`-style splice inserts at every character boundary). Likewise a half-deleted block (BEGIN without END, or vice versa) is reported as `None`/"no block", so the orphan marker line and the now-unmanaged text around it are silently left behind rather than flagged as a broken region. The stamped grammar gets this right via `BLOCK._region().find`; the legacy grammar, which is the one every already-adopted project actually carries, has no equivalent validation.

chunk_findings.detail:
When `region.owns(existing)` raises `RegionError` — i.e. the file contains a managed region whose BEGIN/END pair is malformed, e.g. the END marker was deleted or hand-edited — the handler sets `owned = False` with the explicit comment that "a broken region is the operator's file: leave it alone". But control does not leave: it falls through to `if MANAGED_MARK not in existing:`. The surviving BEGIN marker line is ddflow's managed marker (the same `<!-- DDFLOW:MANAGED` text that `MANAGED_MARK` matches, which is why `MANAGED_MARK` is a prefix rather than a whole line), so `MANAGED_MARK in existing` is True, the `kept` return is skipped, and execution reaches `replace_text(path, desired)` — the operator's file is replaced wholesale with the packaged template. Concrete input: a `.claude/commands/implement.md` that the operator customized and whose region reads
`<!-- DDFLOW:MANAGED:BEGIN commands/implement --> …custom body…` with the matching END line deleted. `owns` raises `RegionError`, `owned` becomes `False`, `MANAGED_MARK` is present, and the file is overwritten with `head + region.render(body)`, destroying the operator's command — exactly what the doc comment on `MANAGED_MARK` promises will not happen ("a file ... with a region someone broke, is the operator's"). (If `replace_text` applies its `NewerContent` guard, the same path instead raises `NewerContent` uncaught, since only the owned/splice branch wraps that call.) The `RegionError` handler must return the "kept" result itself rather than relying on the later `MANAGED_MARK` test.

chunk_findings.detail: The collision loop `for n in range(2, 100)` reassigns `dest = root / f"{name}-{n}"` inside `except FileExistsError` but never verifies the new directory was created on the final iteration. Sequence: `n=2` tries `name` and, on collision, sets `dest = name-2`; `n=3` tries `name-2` and sets `name-3`; … so the candidates `name-2 … name-98` are tried, and on the `n=99` collision `dest` is set to `name-99`, which is never `mkdir`-ed, then the loop exits. With 98 pre-existing `name*` directories, execution falls through and uses the already-existing `name-99` directory: `shutil.copy2`/`replace_text` then overwrite the previous backup's files and manifest. Input: a caller repeatedly invoking `make_backup` with the same explicit `name` (or a clock that doesn't advance) 99 times; the 99th call silently destroys the 98th call's copies. The comment "two backups in one clock tick keep their own directories" shows this exhaustion case is the loop's whole purpose.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/backups.py make_backup (mkdir retry loop)

chunk_findings.detail: For a file outside the repo, `stored = "_outside/" + f.as_posix().lstrip("/")`; for a file inside the repo, `stored = f.relative_to(repo).as_posix()`. These two namespaces are not disjoint: if the project contains a top-level directory literally named `_outside`, then the in-project file `<repo>/_outside/notes.txt` is stored as `_outside/notes.txt`, which is exactly the key an outside file `/notes.txt` maps to. Input: `make_backup(repo, [repo/"_outside"/"notes.txt", Path("/notes.txt")], ...)` writes both to `dest/_outside/notes.txt`, so the second `shutil.copy2` overwrites the first, and `manifest.json` gets two entries with identical `"stored": "_outside/notes.txt"` — a restore from that manifest cannot distinguish them, so one file's original content is lost.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor moves the backup API out of `upgrade_apply` into `services/backups.py`, and re-imports `MANIFEST`, `backup_name` and `make_backup` specifically so that existing importers of `ddflow.services.upgrade_apply` keep working (that is what the `# noqa: F401 -- the backups' home` comment documents). The same diff deletes the module-level constant `BACKUPS = ".ddflow/backups"`, but that name is *not* included in the compat re-export. Any caller of the form `from ddflow.services.upgrade_apply import BACKUPS`, or any code (test, tooling, restore/list helper) reaching for `upgrade_apply.BACKUPS`, now fails with `ImportError`/`AttributeError`, while its three sibling names still resolve — so the shim is incomplete. Either add `BACKUPS` to the re-export alongside `MANIFEST`/`backup_name`/`make_backup`, or confirm there is genuinely no remaining consumer of the old constant (note the same concern applies to any in-file use of `BACKUPS` left in code outside this hunk, which would become a `NameError` at runtime rather than an import error).
