chunk_findings.detail:
The closing-delimiter search starts one character too late for an empty front-matter block. `text.find("\n---\n", 4)` skips index 3, but for a file that begins with an *empty* YAML block the closing `\n---\n` is at index 3 (the newline that terminates the opening `---` is the leading newline of the closing delimiter). Input: a command template whose content is `"---\n---\n# /implement\n..."` (front matter present but empty, a legal slash-command file). The scan returns `-1`, so the function takes the `return "", text` fallback and treats the entire template — including the `---` block — as `body`. `_write_command` then computes `desired = head + region.render(body)` with `head == ""`, writing

```
<!-- ddflow:begin commands/implement -->
---
---
# /implement
...
```

i.e. the front matter is now *inside* the managed region, below the begin line, which both violates the invariant the helper documents ("the managed region starts after the front matter so a slash command's `---` block stays first in the file") and yields an invalid slash command (the parser requires `---` on line 1). Starting the search at 3 — or 0 — finds the closing delimiter and produces the intended `head="---\n---\n"`, `body="# /implement\n..."`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py `_split_front_matter`

chunk_findings.detail: `_run_instructions` now calls `AD.refresh_docs(repo, only=paths, backup=False)`, unconditionally disabling the "refresh docs backs up first" guarantee that is the point of this change, on the assumption that the upgrade has already made an equivalent backup. That assumption is not enforced here: `make_backup` is imported into this module only as a re-export (the `# noqa: F401 -- the backups' home` on the new import shows nothing in `upgrade_apply.py` calls it), and the paths handed to `refresh_docs` are the plan's *instruction* item paths (`paths = [i["path"] for i in items]`), not a file set this module has verified was copied. Concrete inputs where the file is therefore rewritten with no copy anywhere: (a) a project configured with the supported `[upgrade] backups = "none"` mode (`BACKUP_MODES` is unchanged and still includes `"none"`) that runs `ddflow upgrade --apply` over a stale/legacy doc or rule file; (b) any doc/rule file that `refresh_docs` rewrites but that the caller's backup set did not enumerate (the caller backs up its own changed-file list, while `refresh_docs` migrates managed blocks in whatever `only=` paths the plan classified as instructions). In both cases the file the user is asked to trust the new backup for is the one file without one; passing `backup=False` should be conditional on the caller having actually recorded those exact paths in a backup.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_apply.py:_run_instructions

chunk_findings.detail:
The legacy branch extracts the block with unpaired `index()` calls and never checks that the end marker follows the begin marker:

```python
if has_legacy_block(existing):
    head = existing[: existing.index(LEGACY_BEGIN)]
    tail = existing[existing.index(LEGACY_END) + len(LEGACY_END) :]
    replace_text(path, head + section.strip() + tail)
```

This branch is exactly the one reached for a legacy-marker file: `BLOCK.owns(existing)` is False there (that is why the legacy branch exists at all), and `has_legacy_block` is a membership test for the two marker strings, not an order/pair check. Given a docs file whose markers are reversed — e.g. the finding-2 text `"<!-- DDFLOW:END -->\nnotes\n<!-- DDFLOW:BEGIN (managed — edits inside this block are overwritten) -->"`, produced when a user reorders sections or an END is left over from a previous block — `index(LEGACY_END)` is smaller than `index(LEGACY_BEGIN)`, so `head` runs past the END marker and `tail` begins inside the old region; `head + section.strip() + tail` duplicates the prose and leaves the old END marker embedded in the middle of the file instead of migrating it.

The earlier fix for the identical pattern only hardened `block_body` (its reversed-marker probe `test_reversed_legacy_markers_are_a_broken_block_not_an_empty_one` exercises `block_body`), and `_upsert_block` never calls `block_body` on `existing` — it re-slices `existing` here directly. So that probe does not answer this call site.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py:_upsert_block (the `has_legacy_block(existing)` branch)

chunk_findings.detail:
`doc_state` documents a contract for the no-region case: *"else legacy (nothing says whether a person touched it, so the caller backs it up)"*. Its writing caller `_write_driver` does not honor it. It only takes a `.local-edits` copy when `state == DOC_EDITED`:

```python
note = ""
if state == DOC_EDITED:
    aside = local_edits_path(mine)
    replace_text(aside, existing)
    note = f" (your edits are kept in {aside.name})"
...
replace_text(mine, region.splice(existing, want) if owned else region.render(want))
```

For a driver doc that has no managed region (`doc_state` returns `DOC_LEGACY` when `text != want`) and therefore no stamp, `state` is neither `DOC_NEWER`, `DOC_EDITED`, nor `DOC_CURRENT`, so the backup branch is skipped, `region.owns(existing)` is `False`, and `region.render(want)` overwrites the entire file with the shipped body. Concretely: a project adopted by a pre-header ddflow that hand-edited `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` with project-specific instructions, then runs `adopt --refresh-docs`, gets that file replaced verbatim by the template — the person's text is gone, and the returned message (`"wrote docs/.../implement-phase.md"`) does not even mention it. The same happens if the markers were removed/renamed by an editor: the region is absent, state is `DOC_LEGACY`, and the whole file is clobbered with no `.local-edits` copy. This is precisely the case `DOC_LEGACY` exists to guard, and the asymmetry with the `DOC_EDITED` branch (which does back up) makes the data loss silent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py::_write_driver (the `if state == DOC_EDITED:` backup guard)

chunk_findings.detail: `add` overrides the reported `provenance` to `"missing"` when `state == AD.MISSING`, but `keeps` and `summary` are computed from the raw `provenance` argument, so they can still claim a hand edit exists alongside the `"missing"` provenance in the same record. Concretely: a rules file that does not exist, with the project at the running version (`drifted_by_release == False`), reaches `add(rs.path, AD.MISSING, rs.render(), "hand-edited", OPERATOR)`, producing `"provenance": "missing"` but `"summary": "... differs ... (hand-edited) (a refresh keeps your edits in .local-edits)"`. The file is absent and there are no edits to preserve, so the summary is wrong (and contradicts the `provenance` field of the same item). The `MISSING` case is reachable — the pre-change code special-cased `state == AD.MISSING` for exactly these rules_status entries. The `keeps` suffix should be suppressed (or provenance forced to `"missing"`) before building the summary when `state == AD.MISSING`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:224-238 (`add`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_body` derives its base directory with `path.parents[3]`, which is only correct for the depth of `DRIVER`. `DRIVER` is `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` (3 directories below the repo root), so `path.parents[3]` is the repo root and `_driver_region` receives `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md`. `DELTA`, however, is `docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/claude-code.md` (4 directories below the root), so `path.parents[3]` is `repo/docs` and the call at `_body(repo / DELTA)` passes `ddflow/drivers/deltas/claude-code.md` — the leading `docs/` is dropped. `_driver_region` is written to take the repo-relative driver path (`docs/...`, as evidenced by the correct `DRIVER` call); given the truncated path for the delta it resolves the wrong (or a non-existent) driver, so `_region_body` either raises or extracts a region that cannot equal `templates/deltas/claude-code.md`, making the assertion on line 76 (`_body(repo / DELTA) == (templates / "deltas" / "claude-code.md").read_text()`) fail. A single fixed innermost depth cannot serve both inputs; the base has to be the actual repo root (or `_driver_region` must be fed the original `DELTA` string), not `path.parents[3]` computed from each individual file.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_driver_drift.py:_body

chunk_findings.detail: The added paragraph contradicts the paragraph it is appended to. The unchanged paragraph states that `ddflow adopt --refresh-docs` "rewrites only those docs, the AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md blocks and the agents' native rules -- never the MCP launch, hooks or command files." The new paragraph then says: "The same holds for an edit inside the AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md block and the `/implement` command file," where "the same" is the mechanism that copies the file to `<file>.local-edits` *before the refresh rewrites it*. `/implement` is a command file (`.claude/commands/implement.md`, listed in the very same table as "The slash command that drives the queue" under the `command dirs` row). So the new text asserts that refresh rewrites the `/implement` command file (and therefore preserves hand edits to it via `.local-edits`), while the preceding sentence guarantees refresh never touches command files. A reader who hand-edits `.claude/commands/implement.md` cannot tell from this doc whether the edit is protected by `.local-edits` or simply left untouched because refresh never rewrites command files; one of the two statements is wrong.
chunk_findings.title: README.md (the newly added `.local-edits` / stamped-region paragraph, ~line 720)

chunk_findings.detail: `doc_state` documents the contract for a legacy document explicitly: "else legacy (nothing says whether a person touched it, so the caller backs it up)." `_write_driver` is that caller in the refresh path, but its only backup branch is `if state == DOC_EDITED:`. Concrete failure: a repo adopted by an older ddflow has `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` with no region markers (all pre-header docs are legacy, so this is exactly where hand edits live) and a person has edited it, so `doc_state` returns `DOC_LEGACY` (`at is None` and `text != want`). `_write_driver` then skips the backup branch, `region.owns(existing)` is False for a markerless file, and it executes `replace_text(mine, region.render(want))`, overwriting the hand-edited file in place. No `<name>.local-edits` file is produced, contradicting the doc_state contract and the change's stated intent that "hand edits move to .local-edits" — the user's edits are silently and irrecoverably lost (the legacy case is the one where edits cannot be detected by a stamp, so it is precisely the case that must be copied before overwrite).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py `_write_driver`

chunk_findings.detail:
In the region-update branch, the hand-edit snapshot is written to `local_edits_path(path)` — a path derived only from the file, not from the region. The handler processes one `region` per call and re-reads the file for each region (it has to, since it returns immediately after `replace_text(path, updated)`). For a driver doc that contains two managed regions, both hand-edited, this loses one region's edits entirely:

1. Region A call: `existing` = original file (contains A's and B's hand edits). State is "edited", so `replace_text(aside, existing)` writes both edits to `.local-edits/<file>`, then `replace_text(path, updated)` regenerates region A.
2. Region B call: the file is re-read, so `existing` now contains the regenerated region A and only B's hand edit. `replace_text(aside, existing)` **overwrites** the previous snapshot, so A's original hand edits exist neither in the file nor in the aside.

The user was told for region A that "your edits are kept in <aside>", but by the time the run finishes the aside contains only B's pre-state. The same per-file snapshot collision exists across repeated runs of a single edited region, and the message gives no indication that a prior snapshot was clobbered.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py:1104 (managed-region update path, `replace_text(aside, existing)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`add()` computes `keeps` from the *argument* `provenance`, then overrides only the stored `provenance` field for `AD.MISSING` — the summary still embeds the pre-override value:

```python
keeps = " (a refresh keeps your edits in .local-edits)" if provenance == "hand-edited" else ""
...
"provenance": provenance if state != AD.MISSING else "missing",
"summary": f"{text} ({provenance}){keeps}",
```

For a rules entry that needs attention because the file is absent (`state == AD.MISSING`; the `state != AD.MISSING` override exists precisely because `rules_status` can emit this, and the original code guarded it the same way), `_provenance` is still called with `edited=False, proven=False`, so with no release drift it returns `("hand-edited", OPERATOR)`. The emitted item then says `provenance: "missing"` while its summary reads `"<render> (hand-edited) (a refresh keeps your edits in .local-edits)"` — asserting a hand edit for a file that does not exist and promising that a refresh will preserve edits that were never made. With a release drift the same mismatch appears as `(stale)` against `provenance: "missing"`. The summary should be built from the final provenance (and the `keeps` clause suppressed for `missing`), e.g. compute `final = "missing" if state == AD.MISSING else provenance` before both fields.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_plan.py:243-244 (`add` in `instruction_items`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_body` reconstructs the repo-relative path as `path.relative_to(path.parents[3])`, but `parents[3]` is a fixed index whose meaning depends on how deep the file sits. For `DRIVER = "docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md"` the parents are `[drivers, ddflow, docs, repo]`, so `parents[3]` is the repo root and the relative path comes out as `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` (correct). For `DELTA = "docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/claude-code.md"` there is one extra level (`deltas`), so the parents are `[deltas, drivers, ddflow, docs]`; `parents[3]` is now `docs`, and the resulting relative path is `ddflow/drivers/deltas/claude-code.md` — the `docs/` prefix is dropped. The `_body(repo / DELTA)` call at the changed assertion (and `_body(tree / ...)` for any delta) therefore passes a malformed path to `AD._driver_region`, which cannot resolve the delta's managed region; `_region_body` then gets a `None`/wrong region and the comparison against `templates/deltas/claude-code.md` fails (or silently compares the wrong text). The helper needs to anchor on a stable base (e.g. `path.relative_to(path.parents[-2])` computed from the known repo root, or relative to the repo dir explicitly) rather than hard-coding `parents[3]`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_driver_drift.py:19 (helper `_body`)

chunk_findings.detail: `region.render(...)` (i.e. `AD._driver_region(DRIVER).render`) is the routine that writes the *current* canonical stamp — the same stamp `AD.refresh_docs` writes inside `_adopted_old`. That is exactly what test A (`test_a_local_edit_in_a_driver_doc_survives...`) demonstrates: after `_adopted_old`, changing the body while the header stays at the current stamp yields `provenance == "hand-edited"`, not `"stale"`. It is also why test D has to explicitly rewrite the header (`re.sub(r"fmt=\d+", f"fmt={FORMAT_LEVEL + 1}", ...)`) in order to obtain a non-current stamp. In this test, however, no version is ever set to an older value: `driver.write_text(region.render("# an older driver, as an older ddflow wrote it\n"))` produces a document whose header still carries `fmt={FORMAT_LEVEL}` (current) over a body that differs from the canonical one. Under the very classification test A relies on, that document is "hand-edited" (current version, body/sha mismatch), so the assertion `item["provenance"] == "stale"` cannot hold. To actually exercise a stale/older copy the test must downgrade the header version (e.g. `fmt={FORMAT_LEVEL - 1}`) the way test D upgrades it for the "newer" case.

chunk_findings.detail: The confirmed finding still holds, and the new note actually makes it worse. `doc_state` documents for the no-region case: *"else legacy (nothing says whether a person touched it, so the caller backs it up)"* — i.e. the writing caller must preserve such a file. `_write_driver` never does: the only backup is behind `if state == DOC_EDITED:`, while a `DOC_LEGACY` document reaches `owned = region.owns(existing)` → `RegionError` → `owned = False` and is then destroyed in place by `replace_text(mine, region.render(want))`, with the extra line `note = " (a copy from before headers: nothing says whether it was edited; see the backup)"` asserting a `.local-edits` backup that this function never creates (only the pre-existing, generic `_backup_docs` is referenced, whereas the `DOC_EDITED` path deliberately uses the per-file `local_edits_path`). Concrete input: a driver doc copied by a ddflow old enough to predate the managed region (so `_driver_region(rel)._region().find(text)` returns `None`), whose text differs from the shipped template (`text != want`). `doc_state` returns `DOC_LEGACY`, `_write_driver` writes `region.render(want)` over the file with no `.local-edits` copy, and the user is told to "see the backup" that was never made — the hand-written content is unrecoverable. The triage's probe (`test_a_plain_adopt_over_a_pre_header_driver_saves_the_original`) does not answer this: a "pre-header" driver is one that still has the region markers but no version+sha stamp (handled by the `DOC_EDITED` branch when `region.state` cannot prove it was unedited), not the no-region `DOC_LEGACY` file the contract in `doc_state` is about.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py::_write_driver (the `if state == DOC_EDITED:` backup guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The call is placed *after* every write it is supposed to preserve. In this same function, the `_driver_pairs` loop (new line ~930) has already rewritten the driver docs via `_write_driver`, the `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` loop (new lines ~938-975) has already spliced the managed blocks, and `init_files(repo)` has run, before `if saved := _backup_docs(repo, docs_dir, package_dir, None)` executes at ~979. So the "originals" it snapshots are the post-adopt contents, contradicting its own `# the originals first` comment. Concrete input: run adopt over a repo that already contains `docs/AGENTS.md` and `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` where the file bodies are unchanged but stale/headerless — the preceding loops update/splice them first, so the backup cannot restore the pre-adopt state for any file that was not already captured by the per-file `.local-edits` aside (e.g. a file with no hand edit at all, whose only "original" record this snapshot was meant to be).

chunk_findings.detail: `_write_driver` is not a string-returning function: its own body returns `Refused(f"REFUSED {rel}: {exc}")` on `NewerContent` (new line ~1106). The new call sites append that return value directly into `actions`, a list whose every other element (the old `f"{rel} is current"` / `f"wrote {rel}"` strings, `init_files(repo)` results, and `f"saved the originals in {saved}"`) is a `str`. Concrete input: a driver doc whose recorded header version is newer than the installed template (e.g. the templates were downgraded) makes `_write_driver` return a `Refused` object, so `actions` becomes `[<str>, <Refused>, ...]`; any consumer that joins/renders `actions` as text (`"\n".join(actions)`) raises `TypeError`, and a consumer that special-cases `Refused` at the top level will silently miss this refusal.

chunk_findings.detail: The D-compat 2 guard is implemented only for drivers. The driver loop special-cases `st == AD.DOC_NEWER` and emits a NOTE item ("upgrade ddflow, do not refresh it"), but the rules loop has no equivalent and sends every `rs.needs_attention` entry through `_provenance`, which has no notion of "written by a newer ddflow". Given a rules block whose header records a version greater than the running ddflow (which the stated intent makes possible, since "rules blocks carry a version+sha header"), the rules loop calls `_provenance(drifted_by_release, edited=rs.edited, proven=rs.stamped and rs.state == AD.STALE)`. `rs.state` is the newer state, so `proven` is `False`; with a shipped release (`drifted_by_release=True`) the result is `("stale", AGENT)`, so the plan tells the agent to run `ddflow adopt --refresh-docs` and summarises it as merely stale, which overwrites the newer rules block with this older ddflow's version -- exactly what the driver branch forbids. With `drifted_by_release=False` it instead reports `("hand-edited", OPERATOR)` with the "(hand-edited) (a refresh keeps your edits in .local-edits)" summary, falsely attributing a hand edit to a block that is simply newer. The rules loop needs the same newer-version check that the driver loop has.

chunk_findings.detail: The same commit computes the `newer` flag in the rules-file loop (`RulesState(name, state, block_edited(text), _stamped(text), block_newer(text))`), but the sibling `if rule.form == FORM_BLOCK:` branch for native rule files builds the record with only four positional fields (`rule.path`, `_block_state(got, want_block)`, `block_edited(got)`, `_stamped(got)`) and never calls `block_newer(got)`. `newer` therefore always falls back to its default `False` for native rules blocks. Concretely: an agent-native rules file (e.g. a `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` style FORM_BLOCK surface) whose managed block was written by a newer ddflow (same case that `block_newer` is designed to detect and that the first branch does detect for `AGENTS.md`) is reported with `stamped=True, edited=False, newer=False`. Downstream that combination is exactly the one the field comments describe as "differs is proven to be an unedited older copy unless `edited`", i.e. a safe-to-overwrite stale block, so the higher-format block can be treated as stale rather than newer — the same file gets the correct `newer=True` if it happens to be handled by the rules-file loop but silently loses it here. The two branches read the same kind of stamped block and should classify it identically.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py:560-564 (native `FORM_BLOCK` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `existing = mine.read_text("utf-8", errors="replace")` decodes the file lossily, and the `DOC_EDITED` branch then writes that string to the snapshot with `replace_text(aside, existing)`, before `mine` itself is overwritten with `region.splice(existing, want)`. The snapshot is the one artifact whose stated job is to keep "what a person wrote", and it is not a byte-faithful copy. Concrete input: `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` hand-edited in an editor that saved it as cp1252, containing a byte such as `0xE9` inside the region body. `doc_state` sees the digest mismatch and returns `DOC_EDITED`, so the file is copied to `implement-phase.md.local-edits`; but `existing` holds `U+FFFD` at that position, so both the `.local-edits` file and the rewritten doc contain the replacement character and the original byte survives nowhere. Reading/writing the snapshot as bytes (or at least decoding without `errors="replace"` for the snapshot) is required for the backup to actually preserve the edit it is supposed to preserve.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/adopt.py `_write_driver` (the `state == DOC_EDITED` snapshot branch)

chunk_findings.detail:
This test runs the *upgrade* (`go(old, "instructions")`) against the raw 0.1.3 fixture, whose driver `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` is a pre-header (legacy, unstamped) document with no managed markers — the exact place finding 2 says hand edits live — and then asserts:

```python
assert AD._driver_region(DRIVER).owns((old / DRIVER).read_text())
assert not (old / (DRIVER + ".local-edits")).exists()
```

i.e. it asserts that a legacy driver is overwritten in place with **no** `.local-edits` snapshot. That is precisely the buggy behaviour finding 2 was confirmed to fix ("`doc_state` documents the contract … the caller backs it up", but `_write_driver` only backs up on `DOC_EDITED`). The probe cited for that fix, `tests/test_compat_adopt.py::test_a_plain_adopt_over_a_pre_header_driver_saves_the_original`, only exercises a **plain adopt**, so it does not answer the upgrade path; if the fix were actually applied in `_write_driver`, this new assertion would have to fail. The rest of the diff corroborates this: `_adopted_old` has to call `AD.refresh_docs(old, backup=False)` specifically so that the fixture's own legacy driver docs are *not* snapshotted during setup — which only makes sense if a normal refresh (backup enabled) does back up legacy docs. And the sibling test `test_a_local_edit_in_a_driver_doc_survives_to_local_edits_and_is_reported` shows the upgrade path does use the backup-enabled writer (it expects `docs/.../implement-phase.md.local-edits`), so the upgrade cannot be using `backup=False` to explain the missing file here. Net effect: a repo adopted by an older ddflow whose `implement-phase.md` carries unmarked hand edits gets those edits silently destroyed on `… instructions`, and this test locks that in as expected behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail: The confirmed finding still holds, and the new note actually makes it worse. `doc_state` documents for the no-region case: *"else legacy (nothing says whether a person touched it, so the caller backs it up)"* — i.e. the writing caller must preserve such a file. `_write_driver` never does: the only backup is behind `if state == DOC_EDITED:`, while a `DOC_LEGACY` document reaches `owned = region.owns(existing)` → `RegionError` → `owned = False` and is then destroyed in place by `replace_text(mine, region.render(want))`, with the extra line `note = " (a copy from before headers: nothing says whether it was edited; see the backup)"` asserting a `.local-edits` backup that this function never creates (only the pre-existing, generic `_backup_docs` is referenced, whereas the `DOC_EDITED` path deliberately uses the per-file `local_edits_path`). Concrete input: a driver doc copied by a ddflow old enough to predate the managed region (so `_driver_region(rel)._region().find(text)` returns `None`), whose text differs from the shipped template (`text != want`). `doc_state` returns `DOC_LEGACY`, `_write_driver` writes `region.render(want)` over the file with no `.local-edits` copy, and the user is told to "see the backup" that was never made — the hand-written content is unrecoverable. The triage's probe (`test_a_plain_adopt_over_a_pre_header_driver_saves_the_original`) does not answer this: a "pre-header" driver is one that still has the region markers but no version+sha stamp (handled by the `DOC_EDITED` branch when `region.state` cannot prove it was unedited), not the no-region `DOC_LEGACY` file the contract in `doc_state` is about.

chunk_findings.detail: The call is placed *after* every write it is supposed to preserve. In this same function, the `_driver_pairs` loop (new line ~930) has already rewritten the driver docs via `_write_driver`, the `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` loop (new lines ~938-975) has already spliced the managed blocks, and `init_files(repo)` has run, before `if saved := _backup_docs(repo, docs_dir, package_dir, None)` executes at ~979. So the "originals" it snapshots are the post-adopt contents, contradicting its own `# the originals first` comment. Concrete input: run adopt over a repo that already contains `docs/AGENTS.md` and `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` where the file bodies are unchanged but stale/headerless — the preceding loops update/splice them first, so the backup cannot restore the pre-adopt state for any file that was not already captured by the per-file `.local-edits` aside (e.g. a file with no hand edit at all, whose only "original" record this snapshot was meant to be).

chunk_findings.detail: `_write_driver` is not a string-returning function: its own body returns `Refused(f"REFUSED {rel}: {exc}")` on `NewerContent` (new line ~1106). The new call sites append that return value directly into `actions`, a list whose every other element (the old `f"{rel} is current"` / `f"wrote {rel}"` strings, `init_files(repo)` results, and `f"saved the originals in {saved}"`) is a `str`. Concrete input: a driver doc whose recorded header version is newer than the installed template (e.g. the templates were downgraded) makes `_write_driver` return a `Refused` object, so `actions` becomes `[<str>, <Refused>, ...]`; any consumer that joins/renders `actions` as text (`"\n".join(actions)`) raises `TypeError`, and a consumer that special-cases `Refused` at the top level will silently miss this refusal.

chunk_findings.detail: The D-compat 2 guard is implemented only for drivers. The driver loop special-cases `st == AD.DOC_NEWER` and emits a NOTE item ("upgrade ddflow, do not refresh it"), but the rules loop has no equivalent and sends every `rs.needs_attention` entry through `_provenance`, which has no notion of "written by a newer ddflow". Given a rules block whose header records a version greater than the running ddflow (which the stated intent makes possible, since "rules blocks carry a version+sha header"), the rules loop calls `_provenance(drifted_by_release, edited=rs.edited, proven=rs.stamped and rs.state == AD.STALE)`. `rs.state` is the newer state, so `proven` is `False`; with a shipped release (`drifted_by_release=True`) the result is `("stale", AGENT)`, so the plan tells the agent to run `ddflow adopt --refresh-docs` and summarises it as merely stale, which overwrites the newer rules block with this older ddflow's version -- exactly what the driver branch forbids. With `drifted_by_release=False` it instead reports `("hand-edited", OPERATOR)` with the "(hand-edited) (a refresh keeps your edits in .local-edits)" summary, falsely attributing a hand edit to a block that is simply newer. The rules loop needs the same newer-version check that the driver loop has.

chunk_findings.detail: The same commit computes the `newer` flag in the rules-file loop (`RulesState(name, state, block_edited(text), _stamped(text), block_newer(text))`), but the sibling `if rule.form == FORM_BLOCK:` branch for native rule files builds the record with only four positional fields (`rule.path`, `_block_state(got, want_block)`, `block_edited(got)`, `_stamped(got)`) and never calls `block_newer(got)`. `newer` therefore always falls back to its default `False` for native rules blocks. Concretely: an agent-native rules file (e.g. a `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` style FORM_BLOCK surface) whose managed block was written by a newer ddflow (same case that `block_newer` is designed to detect and that the first branch does detect for `AGENTS.md`) is reported with `stamped=True, edited=False, newer=False`. Downstream that combination is exactly the one the field comments describe as "differs is proven to be an unedited older copy unless `edited`", i.e. a safe-to-overwrite stale block, so the higher-format block can be treated as stale rather than newer — the same file gets the correct `newer=True` if it happens to be handled by the rules-file loop but silently loses it here. The two branches read the same kind of stamped block and should classify it identically.

chunk_findings.detail: `existing = mine.read_text("utf-8", errors="replace")` decodes the file lossily, and the `DOC_EDITED` branch then writes that string to the snapshot with `replace_text(aside, existing)`, before `mine` itself is overwritten with `region.splice(existing, want)`. The snapshot is the one artifact whose stated job is to keep "what a person wrote", and it is not a byte-faithful copy. Concrete input: `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` hand-edited in an editor that saved it as cp1252, containing a byte such as `0xE9` inside the region body. `doc_state` sees the digest mismatch and returns `DOC_EDITED`, so the file is copied to `implement-phase.md.local-edits`; but `existing` holds `U+FFFD` at that position, so both the `.local-edits` file and the rewritten doc contain the replacement character and the original byte survives nowhere. Reading/writing the snapshot as bytes (or at least decoding without `errors="replace"` for the snapshot) is required for the backup to actually preserve the edit it is supposed to preserve.

chunk_findings.detail:
This test runs the *upgrade* (`go(old, "instructions")`) against the raw 0.1.3 fixture, whose driver `docs/ddflow/drivers/implement-phase.md` is a pre-header (legacy, unstamped) document with no managed markers — the exact place finding 2 says hand edits live — and then asserts:

```python
assert AD._driver_region(DRIVER).owns((old / DRIVER).read_text())
assert not (old / (DRIVER + ".local-edits")).exists()
```

i.e. it asserts that a legacy driver is overwritten in place with **no** `.local-edits` snapshot. That is precisely the buggy behaviour finding 2 was confirmed to fix ("`doc_state` documents the contract … the caller backs it up", but `_write_driver` only backs up on `DOC_EDITED`). The probe cited for that fix, `tests/test_compat_adopt.py::test_a_plain_adopt_over_a_pre_header_driver_saves_the_original`, only exercises a **plain adopt**, so it does not answer the upgrade path; if the fix were actually applied in `_write_driver`, this new assertion would have to fail. The rest of the diff corroborates this: `_adopted_old` has to call `AD.refresh_docs(old, backup=False)` specifically so that the fixture's own legacy driver docs are *not* snapshotted during setup — which only makes sense if a normal refresh (backup enabled) does back up legacy docs. And the sibling test `test_a_local_edit_in_a_driver_doc_survives_to_local_edits_and_is_reported` shows the upgrade path does use the backup-enabled writer (it expects `docs/.../implement-phase.md.local-edits`), so the upgrade cannot be using `backup=False` to explain the missing file here. Net effect: a repo adopted by an older ddflow whose `implement-phase.md` carries unmarked hand edits gets those edits silently destroyed on `… instructions`, and this test locks that in as expected behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail: `TickCtx` is passed by reference into the worker thread (`_call` does `t.resolve()(ctx)`), and the documented cooperative-stop contract is that a tick loops on `ctx.expired()` / `ctx.remaining()`. But as soon as the hard wait expires, `_call` returns `CUT` while the worker is still running, and the very next statement in `_run_due` is `ctx.deadline = None`. From that instant the orphaned worker sees `remaining() == inf` and `expired() == False`, i.e. the exact opposite of "you are over budget, stop". Concrete failure: register a tick with `budget_s=1.0` whose target is `while not ctx.expired(): work()`; at t≈1.0s `_call` cuts it and returns, `ctx.deadline` is nulled, the worker's next `expired()` check returns False, and it keeps looping to completion (or forever), consuming CPU/IO and potentially mutating `.ddflow` state after the pass already recorded it as `cut`. The same stale `ctx` also means that while subsequent ticks run, the orphan reads *their* `begun + budget` deadline, so it can observe a budget that belongs to a different tick. The cooperative-stop mechanism is defeated precisely in the case it exists for.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ticks.py `_run_due` (the `ctx.deadline = None` reset after `_call`)

chunk_findings.detail: `_claim` marks every due stateful tick with `last_at = now` and `status = "running"` before any of them execute, and the only path that undoes a claim is the pass-budget `_release`. Any abort after the claim but before a tick is processed leaves the tick permanently "claimed but never run". The pass loop can abort with an exception that is not swallowed: `threading.Thread.start()` in `_call` is outside the `try/except BaseException` (which only wraps `work`), so a `RuntimeError: can't start new thread` on a thread-limited host propagates to `run_due`, which returns a single `"*"` FAILED result — meanwhile every other due tick is recorded as `last_at=now, status="running"` and will not be attempted again until `every_s` elapses, and `status()`/the doctor line report it as running indefinitely. A `KeyboardInterrupt` during a multi-second tick (e.g. Ctrl+C while `flow.sample` is waiting) does the same, since `run_due` only catches `LockTimeout`/`OSError`/`Exception`. This contradicts the stated behaviour that a tick not reached is "not marked as run, so the next command picks it up"; the deferral path releases the claim, the abort path does not.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ticks.py `_run_due` / `_claim` (claim-all-upfront with no abort unwinding)

chunk_findings.detail: The test is meant to prove that a tick already claimed by another command (`status: "running"`) is skipped. But it seeds the state with `"last_at": clock.now - 5` while the tick has `every_s=60`. Since `now - last_at = 5 < 60`, the tick is not due *by time alone*, so `run(...)` returns `[]` and `log == []` regardless of whether the implementation looks at the `"running"` claim at all. The test therefore passes even if the "claimed before it runs" logic is completely removed or broken — it is non-discriminating for the exact safety property the change is built around. To actually exercise the claim path it must make the tick time-due, e.g. seed `"last_at": clock.now - 3600` (older than `every_s`), so that only the `"running"` status can explain the skip. As written, it gives false assurance that per-machine claiming works. (Note a symmetric risk exists in `test_load_runs_the_ticks_and_the_flow_sample_is_taken_once_per_interval`, whose `first` non-empty assertion can be satisfied by the prior `config --set` invocation's own sample rather than by `_load`; I am not confident enough about that ordering to report it.)
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_local_ticks.py::test_a_tick_another_command_already_claimed_is_not_run_twice

chunk_findings.detail:
A tick that overruns is "CUT", but `_call` never joins the worker thread, and the main loop immediately mutates the *same* `TickCtx` the straggler still holds: `ctx.deadline = None` right after `_call` returns, and later `ctx.deadline = begun + budget` of the *next* tick. `TickCtx.expired()`/`remaining()` — documented as the cooperative-cancellation contract ("A tick that loops checks this between steps and stops cleanly when True") — therefore stop describing the straggler's own budget: after the pass it sees `deadline is None` → `remaining() == inf` → `expired()` is permanently `False`. Concretely, a tick with `budget_s = 10`

    def t(ctx):
        data = slow_fetch()          # e.g. blocks 60 s, ignores the deadline
        if ctx.expired():            # expected True here: this tick was cut at 10 s
            return "aborted"
        heavy_process(data)          # runs anyway, another 60 s

is cut at 10 s and reported `status: cut`, yet `heavy_process(data)` still executes because the main thread reset `ctx.deadline` to `None` before the straggler ever looked at it. The command "goes on without it" only in the sense that the caller stops waiting; the tick itself has no way to observe that its budget was exceeded, so a cut tick can keep doing expensive work (and mutating `ctx.state`/`ctx.events`) indefinitely. Same contamination when a *later* tick's deadline is installed while the previous straggler is alive: it reads a deadline that belongs to someone else. Fix would be to leave the expired deadline in place (or give each run its own ctx), not to null it out while unjoined workers may still read it.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_release` unconditionally clears the state row for a name it once claimed, without checking that the row still belongs to this pass's claim:

```
row.pop("last_at", None)
row["status"] = DEFERRED
```

Any claim made by another command in the meantime is destroyed. Concrete interleaving: process A's pass claims tick X (`every_s=5`, e.g. a quota meter) at t0 (`last_at=t0`, `status="running"`). A's pass then spends its whole budget on other ticks, so X hits `left <= 0` and is left in `pending` instead of being run. At t0+6 process B starts, reads X as due (6 >= 5), claims it (`last_at=t0+6`), runs it, and `_record`s `status="ran", last_at=t0+6`. A's `finally` then executes `_release(X)`, which pops `last_at` and overwrites `status` with `"deferred"`. B's completed run is erased: `status(repo)` reports the tick as deferred/failed rather than ran, and the next command sees X due again and re-runs it immediately (duplicate execution, exactly what the claim mechanism exists to prevent). A guard such as "only release when the row's `last_at`/`status` still match the claim I made" (or holding the claim token) is needed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/ticks.py `_release` (called from `_run_due`'s `finally`)

chunk_findings.detail: For an `every_s == 0` tick the outcome is written only when it does not succeed, but nothing ever clears that row on a later success, so `status()` permanently reports the stale failure. This affects the only shipped tick, `flow.sample` (`every_s=0`): if it raises (or `TickUnavailable`) on one pass, `_record` writes `{"status": "failed"/"unavailable", "detail": ..., "took_s": ...}` with no `last_at`; on every later pass the tick runs fine, `status_ == RAN`, so the gate skips `_record`, and `status()` keeps returning `last.get("status", ...)` = `"failed"` with the old detail indefinitely. The observable result contradicts the docstring ("what each registered tick last did … reports `every-pass`"): given one transient failure of `flow.sample`, `status(repo)` will say `failed` for that tick forever even though it has succeeded on every pass since. A success for a `every_s == 0` tick needs to at least reset the row's `status` (without necessarily rewriting the file every pass), or `status()` must not treat an old failure row as current.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_release` unconditionally does `row.pop("last_at")` and `row["status"] = DEFERRED` on the tick's row without verifying that the row still belongs to *this* process's claim. A claim is not tagged with any owner/token; the only thing identifying it is `last_at == now`. Two commands on the same repo therefore can interleave such that command A's deferred-tick hand-back destroys command B's concurrent claim (or B's completed record).

Concrete scenario: tick `S` (every_s=1, budget_s=60, target sleeps) and tick `T` (every_s=1, budget_s=60) registered, default `pass_budget_s=15`. Command A at wall time t0 claims both (last_at=t0, status running) and reaches `S`; `_call` cuts it at ~15s, so `left <= 0` and `T` is appended DEFERRED and left in `pending`. Meanwhile command B starts at t0+2: `_split_due`/`_claim` see `T` with last_at=t0 and `2 >= every_s=1`, so B claims `T` (last_at=B_now, status running) and runs it to completion, recording `status: RAN` with last_at=B_now. When A's loop exits at ~t0+15, the `finally` calls `_release(path, T)`, which reads the now-B-owned row, pops `last_at`, sets `status: DEFERRED`, and writes. Result: B's successful run is erased (`_record` preserves whatever `last_at` it read, and if A's release lands first, B's record writes a row with no `last_at` at all), `T` becomes due on the very next command despite `every_s=1`, contradicting the "Minimum seconds between two runs on this machine" contract, and `status()` reports DEFERRED for a tick that just ran. This is exactly the two-commands-starting-together case the lock is supposed to serialize; the lock serializes the read/write but not the claim *ownership*, so the later release wins. Fix would require stamping the claim (e.g. an owner/token or claim timestamp) in the row and having `_release` only act when the row still carries this process's claim.

chunk_findings.detail: This probe still does not exercise the "running" claim check it is supposed to cover. The inner pass runs from inside the hook with the fake clock un-advanced, so `now - last_at == 0 < every_s == 60`: `run(...) == []` and `inner == [[]]` hold on the interval check alone, exactly as in the original seeded test. The status check is only load-bearing precisely when the interval check cannot cover for it — a tick that outruns its own `every_s` (claim at `t0`, another pass at `t0 + 61` with `every_s == 60`), or an `every_s == 0` tick (which this suite asserts is *never* claimed: `test_a_zero_interval_tick_is_not_recorded_while_it_succeeds`). Neither case is exercised. Concretely, delete the read of the `"running"` status (or change the hard-coded `"running"` literal on the writer/reader side) and both this test and the original one still pass, so the claim/status handling the finding called out remains untested. A probe that advanced `clock` past `every_s` (or used `every_s=0` with a claimed tick) before the nested pass would answer it.

chunk_findings.detail: The `assert first, "the first load took a sample"` does not come from `_load` at all: the preceding `run_cli(proj, "config", "--set", "schedule.parallel", "auto")` is itself a command whose `_load` samples under `auto` — the sibling test relies on exactly this (`shutil.rmtree(proj / ".ddflow/local", ...)  # the set itself sampled, under auto`). So the ring is already populated before the first `_load(proj)`, `first` is non-empty for free, and `second == first` holds trivially if `_load` takes no samples. In fact all three call-site tests pass with the entire call site removed: this one (sample already on disk, no new sample), `test_load_does_not_sample_when_parallel_is_not_auto` (a negative assertion), and `test_load_survives_a_registry_that_raises` (monkeypatched `run_due` never called, `_load` still returns non-None values). The section's stated purpose — that `_load` runs whatever is due — is therefore unverified; removing `.ddflow/local` (as the sibling test does) before the first `_load` would fix it.

chunk_findings.detail: The `plan is False` identity check makes the MCP `plan=false` → apply-all contract depend on the exact Python singleton. Any caller that reaches this function with a non-bool falsy value (`plan=0`, `plan=None`, or the string `"false"` if a transport/deserializer passes JSON strings through) falls into the plan branch instead of the apply branch, silently returning a plan exit code (0/1) where the caller expected an apply. The docstring explicitly promises "the MCP `plan=false` means `all`", so a value that is falsy but not the `False` singleton breaks that promise without any error. A plain `if apply or plan is False` is fine only if every upstream layer is guaranteed to hand over a genuine `bool`; the diff shows no such validation here.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:999 (`upgrade`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change makes apply mode reachable through `plan=False` (the intent says "api.upgrade apply mode (plan=false refusal removed)", the MCP property now reads `"false applies all"`, and on the CLI the `--plan` default was flipped to `False` precisely so `--apply` reaches `api.upgrade` with `plan=False`). But the MCP API shim keeps `plan=a.get("plan", True) is not False`, which is `True` whenever the caller does not pass `plan`. So a call that follows the new documented contract, `{"apply": "config"}`, invokes `api.upgrade(repo, plan=True, apply="config", ...)` — a dry run — and writes nothing / saves no backup. The visible `payload` lambda right below contradicts this: it selects `UPGRADE_APPLY_PAYLOAD` whenever `a.get("apply")` is truthy, i.e. it promises an `applied` report for exactly the request that the `api` lambda left in plan mode. The two lambdas therefore disagree about the mode for `{"apply": "..."}` unless the api happens to let `apply` override `plan`, in which case the CLI's own signal (`--apply` → `plan=False`) would be pointless. To be consistent with the CLI and the payload, the shim needs to force `plan=False` when `apply` is supplied (e.g. `plan=False if a.get("apply") else (a.get("plan", True) is not False)`). Without it, `ddflow_upgrade` with `apply` set reports success but performs only the plan.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/maintenance.py — `ddflow_upgrade` "api" lambda / `plan` argument

chunk_findings.detail: The tool-level description and the `plan` property description now contradict each other about when the tool writes. The description says "Writes nothing unless `apply` is given: then it does the plan after saving originals to .ddflow/backups", while the `plan` property says "Dry run (default); false applies all." Both cannot be true: a call of `{"name":"ddflow_upgrade","arguments":{"plan":false}}` is described by one as writing nothing (no `apply` given) and by the other as applying everything. Worse, the schema leaves the precedence undefined when both are supplied: `{"plan":false,"apply":"config"}` is described by `plan` as "applies all" and by `apply` as "Categories to apply: all, or a comma list", so a caller that deliberately scoped the change to `config` (asking only for repairs to new knobs) can have instructions/hooks/mcp rewritten and originals dumped into `.ddflow/backups/` because `plan:false` implies all. The input schema exposes no rule for resolving `plan:false` against an explicit `apply` category list, so the destructive path is ambiguous. One of the two descriptions (or a documented precedence, e.g. `apply` wins) must be corrected so the contract is self-consistent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/golden/__snapshots__/test_golden_mcp_tools.ambr (ddflow_upgrade `description` vs the `plan` property description)

chunk_findings.detail: `--apply` is a boolean flag (the code's own help text "choose --plan or --apply, not both" and the README wording "upgrade --apply" treat it as a flag). With `action="store_true"`, `getattr(a, "apply", None)` returns `False`, not `None`, when the flag is absent, so `apply is not None` is always true and the guard collapses to `getattr(a, "plan", False)`. The mutually-exclusive check therefore fires on any invocation where `--plan` is set, even when `--apply` was never given: `ddflow upgrade --plan` prints "ddflow upgrade: choose --plan or --apply, not both" and returns 2, i.e. asking for the plan (the documented, default mode) is rejected. If `--plan` defaults to true (as the previous `getattr(a, "plan", True)` path implies), it is worse — a bare `ddflow upgrade` and `ddflow upgrade --apply` are both rejected with exit 2. The correct test is truthiness of the provided flag (`if apply and ...`), or an argparse mutually-exclusive group; `is not None` only works if `--apply` is a value-taking option whose default is `None`, which contradicts the flag-style message and README usage.

chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/setup.py:cmd_upgrade — `if apply is not None and getattr(a, "plan", False)`

chunk_findings.detail: The `--plan` flag was `store_true` with `default=True`; it is now `default=False` while its help still promises "print the plan (the default: nothing is written)". With argparse semantics a bare `ddflow upgrade` now yields `args.plan == False`, which is indistinguishable from an operator explicitly asking for non-plan. This is exactly the backward-compat case the same change turns into an apply trigger ("api.upgrade apply mode (plan=false refusal removed)"), so any pass-through of `args.plan` into `api.upgrade` makes the default invocation apply the plan (rewriting config/instructions/hooks after backup) instead of printing it. Note the two surfaces changed here disagree on the same logical request: `ddflow_upgrade` with `apply` set but no `plan` computes `plan = a.get("plan", True) is not False` → True, whereas the CLI with `--apply all` and no `--plan` computes `args.plan` → False; the two now call `api.upgrade` with opposite `plan` values for the identical "apply all" request. Either `--plan` must keep `default=True`, or `cmd_upgrade` must normalize the absent flag (the MCP path already does this normalization) — as written the parser alone cannot distinguish "no plan given" from "plan explicitly declined".

chunk_findings.detail: The new top-level tool description states "Writes nothing unless `apply` is given: then it does the plan after saving originals to .ddflow/backups ...", while the sibling `plan` property in the same schema now reads "Dry run (default); false applies all." These two sentences are mutually exclusive: the parenthetical in the change intent ("api.upgrade apply mode (plan=false refusal removed)") confirms the implementation path is `plan=false` → apply. A concrete failure: an MCP client (e.g. an LLM agent) that reads only the tool description will conclude `plan` is a pure dry-run switch and may send `{"plan": false}` (perhaps to "turn off" the plan listing) expecting nothing to be written, but the server will run the whole apply path and rewrite files in `.ddflow/backups/` — exactly the outcome the description says cannot happen without `apply`. The `plan` property doc is the accurate one; the description needs to state that `plan=false` also triggers apply (or the property doc is the wrong one and `plan=false` should remain a refusal), so that the two fields agree.

chunk_findings.detail:
The `--plan` flag's default was changed from `True` to `False`, but `False` is not "unset" in this API — it is the apply-all sentinel. The MCP shim written in the same change uses `None` for "not specified" (`plan=a.get("plan") if isinstance(a.get("plan"), bool) else None`), and the tool metadata it emits says the `plan` property is `"Dry run (default); false applies all."` The API therefore distinguishes three states: `True` = dry run, `None` = unspecified (dry run unless `apply` is given), `False` = apply everything. The parser collapses "unspecified" and "apply all" into the same value: `action="store_true", default=False` yields `args.plan == False` when the flag is absent.

Concrete failure: run `ddflow upgrade` with no flags. argparse produces `plan=False, apply=None`. Since the prior findings' context states the `--plan` default was flipped to `False` so that `--apply` reaches `api.upgrade` with `plan=False` (i.e. `cmd_upgrade` forwards `args.plan` directly), this forwards `plan=False, apply=""` — the exact "apply all" input. `api.upgrade` then performs the upgrade (saving originals to `.ddflow/backups` and rewriting files) instead of printing the plan, contradicting the flag's own help ("print the plan (the default: nothing is written)") and the tool description ("Writes nothing unless `apply` is given"). It also makes the CLI diverge from the MCP path, where an unspecified plan is `None` and stays a dry run. The default should be `None` (the "unspecified" sentinel the MCP shim already uses), not `False`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/parsers/maintenance.py:53 (`--plan`)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten test moved the explicit `plan: true` probe to run after `applied = call({"plan": False})` has already upgraded the `old` fixture, and then weakened the check to `call({"plan": True})["content"] != applied["content"]`. The original assertion (`== planned["content"]`) verified that an explicit `plan: true` returns the same plan as the default call; the replacement verifies only that the two payloads differ, which is true for essentially any outcome. Given the fixture is now up-to-date after the apply, an explicit `plan: true` that wrongly re-applied would return a noop apply payload that differs from the earlier `applied` (which carried `results`), and an explicit `plan: true` that was wrongly refused would also differ from `applied`; both regressions pass this assertion, so the test no longer guards the "plan defaults to the plan" behavior it is named for. To keep the guard, capture the explicit `plan: true` result before the `plan: false` call (compare it to `planned["content"]`) or re-plan on a fresh fixture.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_upgrade_plan.py::test_over_mcp_plan_defaults_to_the_plan_and_false_applies (final assertion)

chunk_findings.detail: The change intent lists three `[upgrade]` config knobs — `backup`, `backup_keep`, `config_changes` — and `_upgrade_apply` resolves only two of them before calling the apply service. It reads `config_changes=getattr(up, "config_changes", "agent")` and `backup=backup or getattr(up, "backup", "local")`, and also threads a CLI `--backup` override through `cmd_upgrade` (`backup=getattr(a, "backup", "") or ""`), but `backup_keep` is never read from `cfg.upgrade` and never forwarded to `UA.apply(...)`; the call only passes `categories`, `confirm`, `config_changes`, `backup`, and `agent`. Given that `cfg` is passed to `UA.apply` yet the other two knobs are explicitly resolved and passed from `cfg` here, the apply service is evidently meant to receive these values rather than re-read `cfg.upgrade` itself, so the asymmetry means the knob is dead: an operator who writes `[upgrade]\nbackup_keep = 2` in `ddflow.toml` and runs `ddflow upgrade --apply` gets whatever default `UA.apply` hard-codes, and the retention setting silently has no effect (same for the MCP `api.upgrade` apply path, which flows through this helper). Either `backup_keep=getattr(up, "backup_keep", <default>)` must be passed here (and, if a `--backup-keep` CLI flag was added alongside `--backup`, read in `cmd_upgrade`), or this helper must stop resolving the other knobs and let `UA.apply` read them all from `cfg`.

chunk_findings.detail: The change documents `[upgrade].backup_keep` (default 10) as a knob that controls how many `.ddflow/backups/<stamp>-...` directories are retained, and the intent states all three new knobs are "read by upgrade --apply". In the only `upgrade --apply` path shown, `_load(repo, agent)` produces `cfg`, and the code forwards exactly two of the three knobs to `UA.apply` (`config_changes=cfg.upgrade.config_changes`, `backup=backup or cfg.upgrade.backup`). `cfg.upgrade.backup_keep` is never read or passed anywhere in this file. Since the two knobs that *are* honored had to be passed explicitly (`config_changes` has no CLI flag at all yet is still threaded through), `UA.apply` evidently does not re-load the config itself; it works only from the values the caller hands it. So setting `[upgrade].backup_keep = 3` in the config and running `ddflow upgrade --apply` will prune with whatever internal default `UA.apply` uses (10) and silently ignore the operator's configured value, contradicting both the README text added in this diff and the stated intent that `backup_keep` is read by `upgrade --apply`.

chunk_findings.detail: `prune` is best-effort by design (`shutil.rmtree(..., ignore_errors=True)`), but the call was placed inside the `try` whose only handler is `except OSError as exc: detail = f"no backup could be written ({exc}); nothing was changed"`. `root.is_dir()` only requires execute permission on the parent, while `root.iterdir()` requires read permission on `.ddflow/backups/` itself, so an execute-only backup dir (mode 0111, e.g. created/owned by another account) makes `is_dir()` return True and `iterdir()` raise `PermissionError`; a concurrent removal of that dir between the two calls raises `FileNotFoundError` instead. In either case a backup that *was* successfully written is reported as "no backup could be written (...); nothing was changed", and the pending items are appended to `failed`, aborting the apply — even though backup creation succeeded and the repo files were never touched. The cleanup's failure should not be funneled through the backup-creation error path (and should not claim no backup exists).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_apply.py (the `try` around `make_backup`/`prune`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test is named/described as proving that config_changes = "operator" plus `--confirm` **applies** the change, yet its first assertion is `assert code in (0, 3), out`. Elsewhere in this same file exit code 3 is defined as a refusal (`test_config_changes_ask_makes_the_cli_refuse_an_unset_knob_too` asserts `code == 3` for the refused case, and the pre-existing test at line 825 asserts `code == 3` for an error). So the assertion cannot distinguish "applied" from "refused". It is also only checked for one of the two knobs it confirms: it asserts `"[acknowledged] knob_changed:worktree.root" in out` and `"[refused] knob_changed:worktree.root" not in out`, but never checks `worktree.max_parallel`, even though it passes `--confirm worktree.max_parallel`. Concrete failure the test cannot catch: if the second `--confirm worktree.max_parallel` is ignored (only `worktree.root` is confirmed), the CLI emits `[acknowledged] knob_changed:worktree.root` and `[refused] knob_changed:worktree.max_parallel`, exits 3 — all three assertions (`code in (0, 3)`, acknowledged-root present, refused-root absent) pass, so a broken confirm path for any knob other than the first goes undetected. The test should assert `code == 0` and that no `[refused] knob_changed:worktree.max_parallel` line is present.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_upgrade_apply.py:894 `test_config_changes_operator_with_a_confirm_applies_it`

chunk_findings.detail: `prune` is best-effort cleanup, but it is placed on the same line of control as the backup write, inside a `try` whose handler produces the message `"no backup could be written ({exc}); nothing was changed"` and marks the whole apply as failed. Because `prune` runs *after* `make_backup` has already returned, any `OSError` it raises is guaranteed to hit a handler that reports something factually false: the backup *was* written (and old ones may already have been deleted by earlier iterations of the prune loop). Reproduction: make `.ddflow/backups/` writable-but-unlistable (e.g. mode `0300`, or a directory left behind by an earlier `sudo` run that the current user can write into but not read). `make_backup` succeeds; `root.iterdir()` in `prune` raises `PermissionError`; the handler reports "no backup could be written (…); nothing was changed", the upgrade aborts, and the operator is told there is no restore point even though `.ddflow/backups/<stamp>-…/manifest.json` exists on disk — so the documented "cost: disk on this machine only, pruned to `backup_keep`" cleanup behavior silently disables `upgrade --apply` with a misleading reason. `prune` should run outside the backup-write `try` (or under its own best-effort handler) so its failure cannot masquerade as a backup failure.

chunk_findings.detail: The row reads: `undo | \`git revert\`, or \`git checkout <tag> -- <file>\``. This is wrong for the mode it describes. The snapshot tag is placed on HEAD, and after committing affected untracked files HEAD is either (a) the new `ddflow: snapshot before upgrade` commit or (b) the user's pre-existing HEAD when there were no untracked affected files. In both cases the upgrade's own edits to tracked files are *uncommitted* — that is exactly why the doc (and local mode) tells you to review the change with `git diff`. `git revert` only reverts commits, so following the documented undo leaves the upgrade's working-tree modifications in place (the upgrade is not undone), and in case (b) the natural instruction "run `git revert`" reverts the user's own last real commit instead, destroying unrelated history the snapshot was never about. The correct undo for uncommitted changes is `git checkout <tag> -- <file>` (as the second alternative says) or `git checkout <tag> -- .`; the `git revert` alternative only makes sense for the untracked-files commit, and there usually is none. A user with no untracked affected files who follows this row reverts an unrelated commit while their upgrade edits remain.

chunk_findings.detail: A snapshot refusal is documented to be reported as a refusal with exit 3 (`config_sections/upgrade.py` docstring: "refused (exit 3) with the reason on a tree with uncommitted changes or without git"), and the exception type is named `BK.SnapshotRefused` for exactly that condition. Here, though, `BK.SnapshotRefused` is lumped into the same handler as lookup/filesystem errors and returned as `O.failed("upgrade", str(exc))`, i.e. the failure exit (1/2 per the `_upgrade` docstring), not `O.refused` (3). Concrete case: run `ddflow upgrade --restore latest` for a snapshot backup while the working tree has uncommitted changes (or git is unavailable), so `BK.restore` raises `SnapshotRefused`; the caller gets exit 1/2 instead of the exit 3 that the snapshot-refusal contract promises, so a wrapper that distinguishes "refused, nothing was touched" from "a step failed" (e.g. `if rc == 3`) misclassifies it, even though the identical condition during `--apply --backup snapshot` is surfaced as exit 3. `SnapshotRefused` should be caught separately and returned via `O.refused`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py:_upgrade_restore (the `except (LookupError, BK.SnapshotRefused, OSError, ValueError)` clause)

chunk_findings.detail: `prune` has been moved out of the `try` block. Previously it sat next to `make_backup` inside `try/except OSError`, so a failure to delete old backups was converted into a clean "no backup could be written (...); nothing was changed" result. Now it is a bare call after the `except` clauses, so any `OSError` it raises (e.g. an old backup file/dir that is read-only or owned by another user, so `unlink` fails) propagates out of `_save` uncaught. The only caller does `backup_dir, why = _save(...)` with no surrounding `try`, so instead of a controlled failure the whole upgrade aborts with an unhandled traceback — after `make_backup` has already written new backup files. Input: a repo whose `BACKUPS` directory contains a stale entry that cannot be removed; `make_backup` succeeds, `prune` raises, `_save` raises, upgrade crashes.

chunk_findings.detail: The status is chosen purely from the requested mode, but `_save` in snapshot mode has two distinct failure exits: `SnapshotRefused` (a genuine refusal) and the generic `except OSError` branch, which returns the message `"no backup could be written (...); nothing was changed"`. In the latter case (e.g. snapshot mode where the local-fallback files cannot be written because the disk is full, or the git command errors with an `OSError`), the caller still labels every todo item `REFUSED` even though nothing was refused by the snapshot policy. The record shown to the user then says the snapshot was refused while the detail string says the backup could not be written, mixing the two semantics.

chunk_findings.detail:
The final assertion

    assert git(old, "show", f"{tag}:{DRIVER}") != (old / DRIVER).read_text()

is vacuous. The `git()` helper returns `subprocess.run(...).stdout.strip()`, so the `git show` side has its trailing newline removed, while `(old / DRIVER).read_text()` keeps it. For any markdown driver that ends in a newline (the normal case), the two strings can never be equal, so this line is always `True` — even if the snapshot had been taken *after* the apply, i.e. even if `tag` captured the post-apply content instead of the pre-apply HEAD. The intended guard ("snapshot names the state before the apply") is therefore not actually exercised by this assertion; the regression it is supposed to catch would pass. Comparing stripped-to-stripped, or using `read_bytes()` against the bytes of `git show`, would make the check meaningful.

chunk_findings.detail: The catch clause treats `BK.SnapshotRefused` exactly like an operational error and returns `O.failed("upgrade", str(exc))`, i.e. exit 1, while the same change documents snapshot refusals as exit 3 ("refused (exit 3) with the reason on a tree with uncommitted changes or without git", `config_sections/upgrade.py`), and the very same function maps the other precondition violation in this feature (`--restore` combined with plan/apply) to `O.refused(...)`, which is the exit-3 path. Concrete scenario: a user runs `ddflow upgrade --restore latest` where the latest backup is a snapshot and the working tree has uncommitted changes (the exact condition the config doc says is refused with exit 3). `BK.restore` raises `BK.SnapshotRefused`, the code catches it at this line, and the process exits 1, not 3. Any caller that distinguishes "refused, tell the user to commit/stash" (exit 3) from "operation failed" (exit 1) — the documented contract for snapshot mode — will misclassify this case. The `SnapshotRefused` case should return `O.refused(...)` (with the exception text) rather than being folded into the generic `O.failed` branch shared with `LookupError`/`OSError`/`ValueError`.

chunk_findings.detail: `make_snapshot` creates a sidecar local backup for every affected file git cannot hold (`elsewhere`: ignored files, files outside the tree, git hooks) via `make_backup(repo, elsewhere, frm, to)`, and it names the snapshot tag from the *same* `backup_name(frm, to)`: `tag = f"{SNAPSHOT_PREFIX}{backup_name(frm, to)}"`. So the sidecar directory's name and the snapshot tag's suffix are the same string (or the sidecar's stamp is one tick newer, since the tag is built first and `backup_name` is called again inside `make_backup`). `newest()` then does `names = [*local_backups(repo), *snapshots(repo)]` and `max(names, key=_stamp)`; Python's `max` returns the *first* maximal element, and the sidecar sorts first, so with equal stamps the sidecar wins, and with a newer stamp it also wins. Concrete input: a snapshot-mode upgrade whose affected files include a git hook (the docstring explicitly says hooks are the typical `elsewhere` case) plus `src/app.py`. `mr = make_snapshot(...)` creates tag `ddflow-upgrade-snapshot/<stamp>-<from>-to-<to>` and sidecar `.ddflow/backups/<stamp>-<from>-to-<to>` containing only the hook. Then `ddflow upgrade --restore latest` → `restore()` calls `newest()`, gets the sidecar name (no `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX`), and dispatches to `_restore_local`, which restores only the ignored/hook files; every git-tracked file in `held` (`src/app.py`) is left in its post-upgrade state. The user asked to restore the latest upgrade and the upgrade's primary payload is silently not restored.

chunk_findings.detail: In snapshot mode the function `return`s from inside the `try` block, so `prune(repo, cfg.upgrade.backup_keep)` is never reached for snapshots — it is only reached on the fall-through local path. Yet the success message itself advertises a local artifact produced by `make_snapshot` (`[REDACTED:host]`, "…for what git cannot hold"), i.e. snapshot mode does write backup files that `prune` is responsible for. Concrete scenario: run `ddflow upgrade --backup snapshot` repeatedly on a project that contains files git cannot hold; each run appends to the local fallback store and `backup_keep` is silently ignored, unlike `--backup local`, which still prunes. The retention policy the user configured never applies in the mode that most often needs it, and the store grows without bound.

chunk_findings.detail: Before this change `prune(repo, cfg.upgrade.backup_keep)` was the second statement inside the `try:` that wrapped `make_backup`, so an `OSError` from pruning was converted into the graceful summary `"no backup could be written (…); nothing was changed"` and no items were applied. In the new code the `try` ends at the `except OSError` clause and `prune(...)` sits after it, so an `OSError` raised by `prune` is no longer caught here. Concrete scenario: the backup directory contains an entry the process cannot unlink (a root-owned file, or one held by `EBUSY`/`EACCES` on the backup volume); `prune` raises `OSError`, which now propagates out of `_save` and out of `_apply` (nothing in this function catches it), so instead of the previous "nothing was changed" failure result the CLI aborts with an unhandled traceback after a backup has already been written.

chunk_findings.detail: `_classify` resolves every input path first, then uses `os.path.lexists(f)` with the comment "a dangling link exists; only a missing path is 'created'". The comment's intent is defeated by `Path(x).resolve()` two lines above: `resolve()` follows symlinks, and for a symlink whose target does not exist it returns the *target* path (e.g. `Path('/repo/config').resolve()` for `config -> missing` yields `/repo/missing`, and `os.path.lexists('/repo/missing')` is `False`). So a symlink in the affected-files list is never classified as itself: it lands in `created` (under the *target's* relative name) or in `elsewhere`, never in `held`/`untracked`, and the symlink path is never committed or tagged. Concrete failure: `config` is a tracked dangling symlink (tree clean, so `_require_clean` passes) and is among the upgrade's affected files; the upgrade replaces `config` with a regular file. `_classify` puts `"missing"` (the resolved target) in `created` and omits `"config"` from `held`, so on `ddflow upgrade --restore` the `git checkout <tag> -- held` call never restores `config` and the removal loop only tries to `unlink` the nonexistent `repo/"missing"` — the restore leaves the post-upgrade regular file in place, i.e. the snapshot silently fails to capture a file the upgrade touches, exactly what the lexists comment was written to prevent.

data.body:
Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). This builds on B-upgrade.2-.5: the manifest, plan, apply and the versioned-repairs registry. Each migration declares since_version, format_level, the artifact kinds it touches, and four functions: detect (pure), plan (a dry-run diff), apply (backup first, writes only through fsio, any log change as corrective events, idempotent) and verify. B-uni-rules-import, the marker-dialect migration from D-doc-regions, the hook-marker migration (B-uni-compat-refs) and the reference rewrites are registered here and are not implemented ad hoc. upgrade --plan lists the pending migrations; --apply runs them per category with consent (D-upgrade-model pieces as accepted). Tests: every migration on fixture projects from older versions is idempotent and verifies.

Split into: B-uni-compat-migrations.1-registry, B-uni-compat-migrations.2-wire, B-uni-compat-migrations.3-seeds.

chunk_findings.detail: After a successful `m.apply(ctx, p.findings)`, the corrective events are appended and (since the exception is caught inside the `with log.transaction():` block, which returns normally) committed. The subsequent fresh detect/`verify` are wrapped together with `apply` in one `try` whose `except Unavailable` returns `Outcome(m.id, UNAVAILABLE, f"could not run: {exc}", ...)`. Concretely: a migration whose `apply` succeeds and writes its files, and whose `m.detect(after)` (or `m.verify(after)`) then raises `Unavailable` (e.g. a transient read failure on a file the migration touched), gets `status="unavailable"` and the detail "could not run: …", even though the migration *did* run and its corrective events are already persisted in the log. A consumer that keys off `UNAVAILABLE` to mean "nothing happened / retry later" (as the module docstring defines it: "one whose detector could not run is `unavailable`") is misled: the pre-apply detector ran fine, the changes are on disk, and the log records them. This is strictly less accurate than the sibling `FAILED` branch, which at least says "applied, but N problem(s) remain"; the post-apply `Unavailable` branch should not reuse the "could not run" wording/status for a migration that already ran.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/migrations/__init__.py:_run_one (the `except Unavailable` branch that wraps `m.apply`/re-detect/`m.verify`)

chunk_findings.detail: The module's contract is that every migration is applied as "detect, plan, BACK UP the files the plan names, apply, ..." (`__init__.py` module docstring), and `run`'s own docstring says "`backup` receives the files a migration's plan names and returns where it saved them; it raises OSError when it cannot, and the migration then writes NOTHING". But `backup` defaults to `None` and `_run_one` guards the backup with `if backup is not None and files:`, so the default call path — a caller who simply invokes `run(repo, log, cfg)` with only the required arguments — takes no backup at all and still calls `m.apply`, rewriting the files the plan names with `where == ""` and reporting `Outcome(..., APPLIED, ..., backup="")`. Concrete scenario: any agent-consent migration whose plan names `config.yaml`; `run(repo, log, cfg)` without the backup argument rewrites `config.yaml`, returns status `applied` with `backup: ""`, and there is no copy to recover from if the result is later found bad, contradicting the "BACK UP ... first" invariant that the rest of the module advertises. Either the parameter should be required, or an omitted backup should be an explicit error instead of a silent skip.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/migrations/__init__.py `run` / `_run_one` (the `backup=None` default)

chunk_findings.detail: The `except Unavailable as exc:` clause wraps `m.apply`, the `ctx.log.append` loop, and the post-apply `m.detect`/`m.verify` calls, and returns `Outcome(m.id, UNAVAILABLE, f"could not run: {exc}", ...)`. `UNAVAILABLE` is documented to mean the detector could not run / nothing was done, but this path is reachable *after* the migration has already run: if `m.verify(after)` (or the fresh `m.detect(after)`) raises `Unavailable` — e.g. the applied change removed a directory or tool the verifier needs, so the verifier now cannot run — the outcome is reported as `unavailable`/`"could not run"` even though `m.apply` already rewrote the plan's files and appended its corrective events (the `where` backup is carried along, which is itself evidence something ran). A caller who treats `unavailable` as "nothing happened" is then wrong about the repository state. The post-apply failures should be classified as `failed` (the migration ran but its result could not be confirmed), not `unavailable`.

chunk_findings.detail: The `try` block does not only contain the post-apply re-detect/verify; it also contains the initial `m.apply(ctx, p.findings)` call. If `m.apply` itself raises `Unavailable` — which is the documented "the migration could not run" signal that the author evidently anticipated by catching it here — the handler returns `Outcome(m.id, FAILED, f"ran, but could not be confirmed: {exc}", ...)` even though the migration never ran and wrote nothing. Concretely, a migration whose `apply` begins with `if not shutil.which("git"): raise Unavailable("git missing")` yields status `"failed"` with detail `"ran, but could not be confirmed: git missing"` and a non-empty `backup`, telling the operator the migration ran (and inviting rollback/retry reasoning based on that) when in fact nothing was applied. The status should distinguish "apply never ran" from "apply ran but its result is unconfirmed" (e.g. `UNAVAILABLE`, as the module docstring reserves for "could not run"), or the `apply` call should sit outside the `except Unavailable` guard so the post-apply detection/verification is the only thing mapped to the "ran, but could not be confirmed" outcome.
