chunk_findings.detail: The failure path collapses all partial progress into a single blanket result. `MG.run` receives the full list of migrations and is caught only *after* it returns or raises; therefore, if it applies the first migrations successfully and then raises `OSError`/`KeyError`/`ValueError` while processing a later one (all three are realistic mid-loop failures — e.g. a migration whose plan references a missing key raises `KeyError`, or an I/O error on the Nth rewrite raises `OSError`), the function returns `[_rec(i, FAILED, ...) for i in items]` for *every* item, including the ones that already ran, rewrote their files, and had backups taken. The user/state layer is thus told those migrations failed when they were actually applied, which contradicts the per-item reporting this function exists to provide (the success path carefully distinguishes APPLIED/UNAVAILABLE/SKIPPED per item). Concretely: `items = [A, B]`, `MG.run` applies A then raises `ValueError` on B → both A and B are returned as `FAILED`; A's changes are on disk and its plan files were backed up, but the record says it failed, so a subsequent `--plan`/retry can treat A as pending and re-run a non-idempotent migration against already-migrated files.

chunk_findings.detail: Both hooks receive a `found` argument and then discard it, recomputing the reference set from scratch with `_rewritable(ctx)`, which re-runs `scan(ctx.repo, vocab)` against the live filesystem. The set that is *planned* is therefore not the set that was *detected*, and the set that is *applied* is neither — each step is an independent scan. Concretely: if the runner applies a filtered subset of the detected findings (interactive selection / `--only`), or if any earlier migration in the same "seed migrations" run writes to a file between the plan pass and the apply pass, `_apply` will call `rewrite(ctx.repo, vocab, refs, backup=False)` on refs that were never in the plan and never approved. The code's own comment asserts the invariant it breaks — "The runner saved the planned files first" — but `refs` at apply time can contain entries the runner never saw, so those regions are rewritten with `backup=False`, i.e. without a backup. Even in the benign case the plan reported to the user (and used to drive backup/undo) can differ from what `_apply` actually changes, e.g. a newly appearing deprecated name in a managed region of a previously-unlisted file is rewritten silently. The fix is for `_plan` to plan from `found` and for `_apply` to act on the planned refs (or re-derive only within the planned file set), rather than re-scanning independently in each hook.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/migrations/refs.py:66-82 (`_plan` / `_apply`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_plan(ctx, found)` and `_apply(ctx, found)` both ignore the `found`/`found: list[Finding]` parameter they are handed and instead re-derive the work by calling `_rewritable(ctx)` again, i.e. they re-`scan(ctx.repo, vocab)` at plan time and again at apply time. The set of files that get rewritten is therefore not the set that was detected, shown to the user, and backed up. Concrete failure: the runner detects at S0, plans at S1, backs up exactly the files in `_plan`'s `Change` list, then calls `_apply` at S2. Between S1 and S2 a file can gain a deprecated name — e.g. a preceding migration in the same `upgrade` run seeds a driver doc or git hook, a concurrent editor saves it, or the plan was rendered interactively and the user took time before confirming. At S2 `_rewritable` now returns that file, and `_apply` calls `rewrite(ctx.repo, vocab, refs, backup=False)`, so the file is rewritten even though the runner never backed it up (the comment at line 88 assumes "the runner saved the planned files first", which is only true for the S1 plan). The pre-rewrite content of that file is gone with no backup, and the change is outside what the plan the operator approved listed. The fix is to make `_plan`/`_apply` operate on the passed-in `found` (or at minimum intersect the S2 scan with the planned paths) rather than re-scanning.

I considered `_verify` returning `[]` unconditionally, but the inline comment states the runner performs a fresh `detect` after apply, and I have no evidence to the contrary, so I am not reporting it.

The final expression is evaluated *after* `m.apply(ctx, found)` has already rewritten `AGENTS.md`, so a fresh `m.detect(_ctx(old))` at that point returns findings for `CLAUDE.md` only: the other test proves the project text `mine: `ddflow doc show`` is never a finding, and the `AGENTS.md` managed region is now current. The filter `f.path == "CLAUDE.md"` is therefore the identity, i.e. `m.plan(_ctx(old), <the full detect list>)` is handed exactly the set that a from-scratch `_rewritable(ctx)` rescan would produce. A `_plan` that still ignores `found` and recomputes (the earlier finding) returns `["CLAUDE.md"]` and passes this assertion unchanged. So the plan half of the earlier MEDIUM finding is not answered by this probe — only the apply half (and only for the "a brand-new file appears after detect" case; it would not catch a rescan that re-reads an already-detected file and picks up a name added to it). To actually exercise the plan path, the call must pass a list that differs from a fresh scan, e.g. pass only the `ddflow_old_next` finding and assert the returned changes exclude the `doc show` rename, or mutate an already-detected file after `detect` and assert its new name is not planned.

chunk_findings.detail: The earlier finding asked that the files actually rewritten be the files that were detected, shown, and backed up. The patch narrows the rewrite to refs whose key is present in the detect-time `found`, but it does not close the hole, because `_plan` and `_apply` each re-`scan(ctx.repo, vocab)` independently (`_chosen` → `_rewritable`) and correlate the two scans only through `_key(f) = f"{f.path}:{f.line}:{f.ref.text}"`. A line number is not a stable identity: any insertion or deletion above a detected reference between the phases changes its key, so the ref no longer matches `{f.key for f in found}`. Concretely: S0 detect finds a managed `oldcmd` at `f.py:10` (`key = "f.py:10:oldcmd"`); between S1 (`_plan`) and S2 (`_apply`) an unrelated line above it is removed (another corrective migration, a formatter, or a user edit), moving it back to line 10. At S1 the key was `"f.py:11:oldcmd"`, so `f.py` was excluded from `_plan`'s `Change` list and therefore never backed up or shown; at S2 the key matches again, so `_apply` calls `rewrite(ctx.repo, vocab, refs, backup=False)` and writes to `f.py` — a file outside the planned/backed-up set, which is exactly the invariant the fix was supposed to restore. The inverse edit (shift between S0 and S1) silently drops a detected, planned, backed-up ref from the rewrite, so the runner's fresh detect flags a still-managed deprecated reference and the upgrade fails for a reference that was supposed to be handled. Correlating two scans by absolute line number makes plan/apply set equality depend on the file not changing at all between phases; the fix only guarantees `apply ⊆ detected`, not `apply ⊆ planned/backed-up`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The earlier finding covers **both** `_plan` and `_apply` ignoring the `found` parameter handed to them (refs.py `_plan`/`_apply`). The new probe only demonstrates the `_apply` half. Its only plan-related assertion is:

```python
assert [
    c.path for c in m.plan(_ctx(old), [f for f in m.detect(_ctx(old)) if f.path == "CLAUDE.md"])
] == ["CLAUDE.md"]
```

but this runs *after* `m.apply(ctx, found)` has already rewritten `AGENTS.md` (the preceding assertion `"ddflow docs show" in AGENTS.md` guarantees it). At that point `AGENTS.md` contains no stale names, so a `_plan` that ignores the passed list and re-derives via `_rewritable(ctx)` re-scans and finds only `CLAUDE.md` — exactly the same single-element result a correct `_plan(found)` would produce from the filtered `[CLAUDE.md]` list. The assertion therefore cannot distinguish the fixed from the buggy `_plan`, so the `_plan` half of the prior finding is not refuted by this probe and still stands. To make it discriminating, `m.plan` would have to be called while `AGENTS.md` is still stale (i.e. before `m.apply`), passing only the `CLAUDE.md` finding, and assert that the returned changes exclude `AGENTS.md`.

chunk_findings.detail: `from_fields` hard-codes the fallback status to `ACCEPTED` instead of taking the kind's default (the way `level`, `priority` and `enforcement` do on lines 104/107/108, and as the docstring on lines 91–92 promises). Given a `KindSpec` whose default status is not `ACCEPTED` — e.g. a kind whose new definitions default to `"proposed"` pending review — and a definition whose fields lack (or, for a definition recorded by an older ddflow, never had) the `status` key, `from_fields` returns `status="accepted"`. `render` then writes `status = "accepted"` into a file that previously carried no status, and `to_fields`/`digest_of` bake `"accepted"` into the digest. The result is that a definition which should surface with the kind's real default is silently re-labelled as accepted, and its digest no longer matches the content an import produced for the same kind's default, so the write/import/drift paths disagree about the record's content — exactly what this module exists to prevent. The docstring's own rule ("a key the fields lack takes the kind's default") is violated only for `status`, which is the anomaly.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/deffields.py:109 (`from_fields`, `status=str(get("status", ACCEPTED))`)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert DF.digest_of(secret, cfg) != DF.digest_of(_fields(RICH), cfg)` is vacuous with respect to what the test claims to guard. `secret` and `_fields(RICH)` are two different field dicts whose bodies differ (`"token ghp_..."` vs. `'Follow snake_case for Python functions.\nUse "quotes" and a \\ backslash too.'`), so the digests are unequal whether or not `digest_of` applies the log profile before hashing. Concretely: patch `deffields.digest_of` to hash the raw, unredacted body (i.e. delete the redaction step), and this test still passes — so a regression where the stored `def.recorded` digest is computed over unredacted content while `logged()` redacts it (or vice versa, making `test_the_digest_is_the_one_a_def_recorded_event_carries` only accidentally consistent because `RICH` carries no secret) goes undetected. The discriminating assertion is an equality against the logged form: `DF.digest_of(secret, cfg) == DF.digest_of(DF.logged(secret, cfg), cfg)`, which fails exactly when the profile is skipped inside the digest. The first line of the test only proves that `DF.logged` redacts, not that the digest path uses it.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_rules_as_events.py::test_the_log_profile_is_applied_before_the_digest

chunk_findings.detail:
`from_fields` treats a field that is *present but null* as a real value instead of as "unset". `fields.get(key, default)` returns the stored `None` whenever the key exists, even with a null value, so the `str(...)` conversions on lines 97, 98, 104, 105, 108, 109, 110 and 111 turn `None` into the literal string `"None"`, and `int(get("priority", spec.default_priority))` on line 107 raises `TypeError: int() argument must be a string...`.

This is reachable exactly in the situation the docstring names ("a definition recorded by an older ddflow still renders"): a record serialised with explicit nulls for unset optional keys (`{"owner": None, "priority": None, ...}`) makes `from_fields` abort rendering of the whole rule file, and for the string keys it silently renders `owner = "None"` / `status = "None"` into `.ddflow/rules/<id>.toml` rather than taking the kind's default. It also breaks the stated write/digest round trip: `to_fields` of the original record yields `owner=None`, while the digest recomputed after the file is parsed yields `"None"`, so a null-only record produces a spurious drift/`def.updated`. The `or`-style normalisation already used for `tags/globs/sources/checks/links` on lines 100-114 should be applied to these scalars too (e.g. `str(get("owner") or "")`).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/deffields.py:97-111 (esp. line 107, `from_fields`)

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback for a missing/`None` `status` is hard-coded to `ACCEPTED`, while every other kind-level default in the same constructor (`level`, `priority`, `enforcement`) is taken from `spec.default_*`, exactly as the docstring on this function promises ("A key the fields lack takes the kind's default, so a definition recorded by an older ddflow still renders"). Nothing in the diff changes this: a definition whose fields omit `status` (e.g. written by an older ddflow that never recorded the key, or a new definition pending review for a kind that defaults to `"proposed"`) is reconstructed as `status="accepted"` rather than the kind's default, so the rendered/re-derived record silently acquires a status it was never given. The inline comment ("as `fileformat.parse`: a file has no other default") does not answer the finding — it only asserts that the parser also hard-codes `ACCEPTED`, which is the same assumption being questioned; the surrounding code and docstring treat a missing key as "take the kind's default", and only `status` deviates.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/guidance/deffields.py::from_fields (`status=str(get("status", ACCEPTED))`)

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `assert DF.digest_of(secret, cfg) != DF.digest_of(_fields(RICH), cfg)` cannot detect whether the `log` redaction profile is applied before hashing, because `secret` and `_fields(RICH)` are different field dicts to begin with (`"token ghp_..."` vs. `'Follow snake_case for Python functions.\nUse "quotes" and a \\ backslash too.'`). Their digests are unequal whether `digest_of` calls `logged(...)` or hashes the raw body, so patching `digest_of` to skip redaction would leave the test green. Nothing in this diff answers it: the body of `digest_of` (`D.digest(logged(fields, cfg))`) still needs a discriminating probe, e.g. comparing `DF.digest_of(secret, cfg)` against the digest of the *same* fields with the secret removed/redacted, rather than against an unrelated record.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_rules_as_events.py::test_the_log_profile_is_applied_before_the_digest

chunk_findings.detail: This prior finding is not answered by the visible part of the diff. The only test that touches the missing-`status` fallback is `tests/test_rules_as_events.py::test_a_definition_missing_keys_takes_the_kinds_defaults`, and it passes `{"title": "Old", "body": "text"}` together with `RULE` only, then asserts `rec.status == "accepted"`. Since `RULE`'s own default status *is* `"accepted"` (as also asserted in `test_the_fields_are_plain_json_with_every_key_present`, where `to_fields` fills `f["status"] == "accepted"` from the spec), that assertion holds identically whether `from_fields` reads the kind's default or keeps the literal `ACCEPTED` fallback — it cannot distinguish the two. `test_a_kinds_own_fields_ride_along` uses `DECISION`, but it round-trips through `to_fields` first, so `status` is always present in the dict it feeds to `from_fields`, and the fallback is never exercised. So a `KindSpec` whose declared default status differs from `ACCEPTED` (e.g. a kind whose new definitions default to `"proposed"`), fed a definition whose fields lack `status` (or one recorded by an older ddflow that never wrote it), still returns `status="accepted"` rather than the kind's default — the behavior the finding describes. The added tests do not probe it; only a test that omits `status` for a non-`accepted` kind would. (I can only see part 2 of the diff, so if `from_fields` was changed in part 1 the code may already be fixed, but the test coverage in this diff does not demonstrate or guard that fix.)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_needed` decides whether the file matches the log by comparing `known.digest` against `DF.digest_of(DF.to_fields(rec, RULE), ctx.cfg)`, i.e. the canonical deffields digest of the file's raw fields. But `_apply` writes a different value: `fields = DF.logged(DF.to_fields(rec, RULE), ctx.cfg)` and then `digest=D.digest(fields)`. Detect and apply do not use the same digest function over the same input (raw fields with the redaction profile applied by `digest_of`, vs. already-redacted fields hashed with the generic `D.digest`). Unless `DF.digest_of(f, cfg)` is exactly `D.digest(DF.logged(f, cfg))`, the digest the migration stores is not the digest the next detect compares against.

Concrete failure: a project with `.ddflow/rules/x.toml` and no `rule:x` record. `detect` emits `record:x`, `_apply` appends a `def.recorded` whose `digest` is `D.digest` over the redacted fields. On the next run (and in the runner's post-apply fresh detect that `_verify` delegates to) `_needed` recomputes `DF.digest_of(raw_fields, cfg)` for the same unchanged file, gets a different value than the stored `known.digest`, sees `known.live and known.digest != digest`, and re-reports `update:x` ("the file differs from the log") even though nothing was edited, appending a spurious `def.updated` on every run. `_verify` returning `[]` unconditionally hides this non-convergence. chunk_findings.detail: `_count` guards the conversion with `r.out.isdigit()`, but `git`'s stdout is not stripped by the helper — the sibling line in the very same function does `(r.err or r.out).strip().splitlines()`, which only makes sense if `r.out` still carries its trailing newline. `git rev-list --count <range>` emits `"5\n"`, and `"5\n".isdigit()` is `False`, so `_count` returns `-1` for every successful rev-list invocation. Concretely, for a worktree that is 5 commits ahead of its base, `tree_work` sets `n_ahead = -1`, and `cleanup._evaluate` then hits `return "" if tw.ahead >= 0 else f"cannot count commits ahead of {wt.base}"` and reports "cannot count commits ahead" for every tree it examines; `t.ahead` is also `max(0, -1) == 0`. The one measurement the change exists to provide therefore reports "unknown" for all readable worktrees, so lease recovery / cleanup can never conclude that a tree's commits are merged. Expected: `n_ahead == 5`; actual: `-1`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py `_count`

chunk_findings.detail: Given a worktree whose branch is 3 commits ahead of its base, `tree_work` calls `_count(path, "BASE..HEAD")`, which runs `git rev-list --count BASE..HEAD`. Git writes `"3\n"` to stdout. `"3\n".isdigit()` is `False` (the trailing newline is not a digit), so the `and` short-circuits and `_count` returns `-1` instead of `3` — the value is discarded before `int()`, which would have tolerated the whitespace. Consequently `tree_work` always reports `ahead = -1` (and `behind = -1`) for any real base, and in `services/cleanup.py` the survey sets `t.ahead = max(0, -1) = 0` and falls into `return "" if tw.ahead >= 0 else f"cannot count commits ahead of {wt.base}"`, so every worktree with a base is reported as "cannot count commits ahead" and never as fully merged, however in-sync it is. The sibling code in the same function confirms the runner returns raw stdout: it explicitly strips it (`why = (r.err or r.out).strip().splitlines()`), whereas `_count` uses `r.out.isdigit()` on the unstripped string. The fix is `r.out.strip().isdigit()` (or `int(r.out.strip())`).

chunk_findings.detail:
The change replaces the local `_status` helper with the unified `W.tree_work(...)` measurement, but accesses the wrong attribute for the file list. Per the stated API of the measurement ("what a worktree holds (readable, dirty, ignored, ahead)"), the collection of work files is exposed as `dirty` — that is exactly how the other new caller reads it: `rec.dirty_files = len(tw.dirty) if tw.readable else -1` in `ddflow/services/leases.py` (around line 834). The two onboard call sites instead read `tw.work`:
`readable, work, ignored = tw.readable, tw.work, tw.ignored` and, in the forced-removal recheck, `if not tw.readable or tw.work or tw.ignored or not W.is_merged(...)`. If `tree_work` has no `work` field (the only work-file accessor anywhere else is `.dirty`), then for any candidate worktree that reaches this code the attribute lookup raises `AttributeError` and the cleanup-survey/forced-removal path aborts instead of reporting (or guarding) the tree. Concrete trigger: run the onboarding/cleanup survey against a repo with at least one existing worktree; evaluating `tw.work` at line 158 (and again at line 300 before a forced `git worktree remove`) fails before any of the safety checks (`work`, `ignored`, `is_merged`) run.

chunk_findings.detail: The fixture deliberately relies on `node_modules/` *not* being ignored (`.gitignore` lists only `.env`, `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `build/`, and `_untracked_cache` comments "not in .gitignore: an untracked cache"), but the tests run the system `git` with no isolation of global/system config — no `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null`, `GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1`, `core.excludesFile` override, or `-c` flags. On any developer machine whose global excludes file (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore` / `core.excludesFile`, where `node_modules/` is an extremely common entry) lists `node_modules`, `git status` reports it as ignored rather than untracked. Then `_untracked_cache` yields no raw status line, so the assertion `assert tw.dirty == ["?? node_modules/"]` receives `[]` and fails, even though `tree_work` behaved correctly. The same global config can also break the suite more broadly (e.g. `status.showUntrackedFiles=no`, which would empty `dirty` in `test_the_one_measurement_equals_the_three_old_ones` and `test_a_clean_tree_...`). chunk_findings.detail: This diff deletes the only place that separates disposable caches from real work (`_CACHES`, `_is_cache`, and the `_status` docstring that justified them). Both call sites now attribute the raw `tree_work` sets directly to the report: `readable, work, ignored = tw.readable, tw.work, tw.ignored` in `_inspect`, and `if not tw.readable or tw.work or tw.ignored or not W.is_merged(...)` in `_force_remove`. Nothing in this diff (or in the described `tree_work` measurement — "readable, dirty, ignored, ahead") restores the cache policy, so a worktree whose only extra content is a cache directory is now treated as holding work. Concretely: a worktree that has merely had `pytest` run in it, leaving `.pytest_cache/` and `__pycache__/` untracked (or `.venv/` ignored), used to be filtered by `_is_cache` and look clean; now `tw.work`/`tw.ignored` are non-empty, so `_inspect` reports the tree as unmerged and `_force_remove` hits the guard and silently refuses the forced removal. The comment being deleted says "nearly every tree here has a `.venv` or a `__pycache__`", so after this change essentially every tree in the report is flagged and the cleanup survey/forced-removal feature stops reclaiming anything. chunk_findings.detail:
The triage's probe does not answer the finding; it is circular.

`uv run pytest tests/test_tree_work.py -k 'ahead or diverged or behind'` selects only the parametrizations of `test_the_one_measurement_equals_the_three_old_ones` whose ids are `_ahead`, `_behind`, `_diverged`. In every one of those, the count under test is only ever compared to another value produced by the *same* code path:

- `tw.ahead` is set by `tree_work` via `_count` (the finding's claim);
- `oracle_recovery` returns `W.ahead(probe)` and `oracle_cleanup` returns `W.ahead(wt)`/`W.behind(wt)` — the `W.ahead`/`W.behind` helpers are the very functions that call `_count`.

So if `_count` is broken exactly as described (`r.out == "2\n"`, `"2\n".isdigit()` is `False`, returns `-1`), then `tw.ahead == -1`, `ahead == -1`, `ahead_c == -1`, and `assert tw.ahead == ahead == ahead_c` still passes; likewise `tw.behind == behind_c` passes with both `-1`. The assertion never pins a literal count, so a `−1 == −1 == −1` collapse is indistinguishable from a correct `2 == 2 == 2`. The probe therefore reports "ahead==2 and behind==1 asserted" for an assertion that appears nowhere in the selected tests.

chunk_findings.detail: `reference_items` documents a hard contract: references "this process had no table to judge" must be surfaced as a note — "'nobody looked' must not read as 'none'". But the *only* path that produces that note is the loop's `f.ref.status == UNCHECKED` branch, which can only be reached after `MR._vocabulary()` returned a non-`None` vocabulary. In the case the docstring is actually about — no vocabulary loaded at all — the function returns `[]` before it ever calls `scan`, so nothing is emitted. Concretely: an in-process caller (an agent/harness invoking the plan without the surface vocabulary wired, i.e. `MR._vocabulary()` returns `None`) planning a repo whose own text contains `ddflow`-deprecated commands gets an identical plan to one whose text is clean — zero "references" items, zero "unchecked" items, no signal that anything was skipped. That is exactly the "nobody looked reads as none" misreading the function promises never to produce, and the `fix` text ("run `ddflow upgrade --plan` … which loads both tables") can never be shown in the situation that most needs it. Either the early return should emit an equivalent "no table loaded, N files looked unchecked" note, or the docstring contract is false.
